Perplexity may be occasioned to some by the great difference, not in words only, but in substance, of the speeches in which Peter is forewarned by Our Lord, and which occasion his presumptuous declaration of dying with or for the Lord. Some would oblige us to understand that he thrice expressed his confidence, and the Lord thrice answered him that he would deny Him thrice before cock-crowing; as after His resurrection He thrice asked him if he loved Him, and as often gave him command to feed His sheep. For what in language or matter has Matthew like the expressions of Peter in either Luke or John? Mark indeed relates it in nearly the same words as Matthew, only marking more precisely in the Lord's words the manner in which it should fall in, Verily I say unto thee, that this day, in the night, before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice. (Mark 14:30.) Whence some inattentive persons think that there is a discrepancy between Mark and the rest. For the sum of Peter's denials is three; if the first then had been after the first cock crowing, the other three Evangelists must be wrong when they make the Lord say that Peter should deny Him before the cock crow. But, on the other hand, if he had made all three denials before the cock began to crow, it would be superfluous in Mark to say, Before the cock crow twice. Forasmuch as this threefold denial was begun before the first cockcrow, the three Evangelists have marked, not when it was to be concluded, but how often it was to happen, and when to begin, that is, before cock-crow. Though indeed if we understand it of Peter's heart we may well say, that the whole denial was complete before the first cock-crow, seeing that "before that his mind was seized with that great fear which wrought upon him to the third denial. Much less therefore ought it to disquiet us, how the three-fold denial in three distinct speeches was begun, but not finished before cockcrow. Just as though one should say, Before cock-crow you will write me a letter, in which you will revile me three times; if the letter were begun before any cock-crow, but not finished till after the first, we should not therefore say that the prediction was false.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: Because they clung to Him inseparably, therefore He saith, "Tarry ye here, while I go away and pray." For it was usual with Him to pray apart from them. And this He did teaching us in our prayers, to prepare silence for ourselves and great retirement.

(de. Fid. Orth. iii. 24.) But seeing that prayer is the sending up the understanding to God, or the asking of God things fitting, how did the Lord pray? For His understanding needed not to be lifted up to God, having been once united hypostatically to God the Word. Neither could He need to ask of God things fitting, for the One Christ is both God and Man. But giving in Himself a pattern to us, He taught us to ask of God, and to lift up our minds to Him. As He took on Him our passions, that by triumphing over them Himself, He might give us also the victory over them, so now He prays to open to us the way to that lifting up to God, to fulfil for us all righteousness, to reconcile His Father to us, to pay honour to Him as the First Cause, and to show that He is not against God.
Gethsemane is interpreted, 'The rich valley;' and there He bade His disciples sit a little while, and wait His return whilst He prayed alone for all.

The Evangelist had said a little above, that when they had sung an hymn they went out to the mount of Olives; to point out the part of the mount to which they took their way, he now adds, Then came Jesus with them to a garden called Gethsemane.

He had accepted the disciples' faith and the devotedness of their will, but He foresaw that they would be troubled and scattered abroad, and therefore bade them sit still in their places; for to sit belongs to one at ease, but they would be grievously troubled that they should have denied Him.

Then Jesus came with them to an estate called Gethsemane.

To one who knows the interpretation of Hebrew names, even the name of this estate which is called Gethsemane is of use for making this place clear, since it is not without reason that the name of the estate too is set down in Matthew and in Mark. But we, passing that over, suggest only this: how Jesus came with his disciples to this estate which is called Gethsemane, taking them out of that place in which he had eaten the Passover with them. For it was not fitting that, when he was being betrayed, he should be seized from that place where he had eaten the Passover with the disciples. But it was fitting also that, before he was betrayed, he should pray and, for praying, should choose a clean place for the prayer; for he knew that, just as air differs from purer air, so does the earth of a holy place differ from that of a holier one, as it is written: "the place in which you stand is holy ground". And you will ask whether, besides the disposition of the one praying, the prayer also becomes cleaner and more acceptable from the place of prayer in which one prays, according to what is written: "my house shall be called a house of prayer", concerning which it is also said elsewhere: "and he heard my voice from his holy temple". And a man of the Jews indeed does not even doubt about such a thing; but he who, because of the teaching of Christ, has withdrawn from "Jewish fables" and from all things that are understood by them in a bodily way, will say that a prayer does not become different from another prayer on account of the place, but rather because it is better to pray with no one than to pray with wicked men. And for the demonstration of this tradition he will use the example that Jesus, in the house of Jairus the priest, being about to pray for his dead daughter, "cast them all outside" and chose only three with him, who had also on the mountain been made witnesses of his transfiguration. For on account of this, in the churches of Christ too, such a custom has held, that those who are manifest in great offenses are cast out from the common prayer, lest a "little leaven" that is not "from a clean heart" of those praying corrupt the whole lump of unity and of concord.

But this meaning also has something that may justly be objected to those who do not understand as they ought, taking occasion to say to their neighbor: "do not draw near to me, for I am clean". Which the Pharisee also did toward the publican who stood far off and beat his breast and said: "Lord, be merciful to me a sinner". Therefore we ought to do this with measure, so that we neither pray with the unworthy for the honor of prayer (according to him who said: "if two of you agree together upon one thing, concerning whatever they ask, it shall be done for them"), nor despise our inferiors, setting ourselves before them through the lapse of boasting (according to him who said: "he who exalts himself shall be humbled"). And these things we have treated on account of what was said: sit here, while I go over there to pray.
For it was not fitting that He should be seized in the place where He had sate and eaten the Passover with His disciples. Also He must first pray, and choose a place pure for prayer.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: And He takes with Him the three, and saith unto them, "my soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death." Wherefore doth He not take all with Him? That they might not be cast down; but these He taketh that had been spectators of His glory.

(Fid. Orth. iii. 23.) Or otherwise; All things which have not yet been brought into existence by their Maker have a natural desire of existence, and naturally shun non-existence. God the Word then, having been made Man, had this desire, through which He desired food, drink, and sleep, by which life is supported, and naturally used them, and contrariwise shunned the things that are destructive of life. Hence in the season of His Passion which He endured voluntarily, He had the natural fear and sorrow for death. For there is a natural fear wherewith the soul shrinks from separation from the body, by reason of that close sympathy implanted from the first by the Maker of all things.

(Lib. 83. Quæst. q. 80.) We have the narratives of the Evangelists, by which we know that Christ was both born of the Blessed Virgin Mary, was seized by the Jews, scourged, crucified, put to death, and buried in a tomb, all which cannot be supposed to have taken place without a body, and not even the maddest will say that these things are to be understood figuratively, when they are told by men who wrote what they remembered to have happened. These then are witnesses that He had a body, as those affections which cannot be without mind prove Him to have had a mind, and which we read in the accounts of the same Evangelists, that Jesus wondered, was angry, was sorrowful.

(de. Civ. Dei, xiv. 9.) Since then these things are related in the Evangelists, they are not surely false, but as when He willed He became Man, so likewise when He willed He took into His human soul these passions for the sake of adding assurance to the dispensation. We indeed have these passions by reason of the weakness of our human nature; not so the Lord Jesus, whose weakness was of power.

These words, He began to be sorrowful and very heavy, are interpreted by heretics that fear of death assailed the Son of God, being (as they allege) neither begotten from eternity, nor existing in the Father's infinite substance, but produced out of nothing by Him who created all things; and that hence He was liable to anguish of grief, and fear of death. And He who can fear death can also die; and He who can die, though He shall exist after death, yet is not eternal through Him who begot Him in past time. Had these faith to receive the Gospels, they would know that the Word was in the beginning God, and from the beginning with God, and that the eternity of Him who begets and Him who is begotten is one and the same. But if the assumption of flesh infected with its natural infirmity the virtue of that incorruptible substance, so that it became subject to pain, and shrinking from death, it would also become thereby liable to corruption, and thus its immortality being changed into fear, that which is in it is capable of at some time ceasing to be. But God ever is without measure of time, and such as He is, He continues to be eternally. Nothing then in God can die, nor can God have any fear springing out of Himself.

(de Trin. x. 10.) I suppose that there are some who offer here no other cause of His fear than His passion and death. I ask those who think thus, whether it stands with reason that He should have feared to die, who banished from the Apostles all fear of death, and exhorted them to the glory of martyrdom? How can we suppose Him to have felt pain and grief in the sacrament of death, who rewards with life those who die for Him? And what pangs of death could He fear, who came to death of the free choice of His own power? And if His Passion was to do Him honour, how could the fear of His Passion make Him sorrowful?

(in loc.) Since then we read that the Lord was sorrowful, let us discover the causes of His agony. He had forewarned them all that they would be offended, and Peter that he would thrice deny his Lord; and taking him and James and John, He began to be sorrowful. Therefore He was not sorrowful till He took them, but all His fear began after He had taken them; so that His agony was not for Himself, but for them whom He had taken.

(non. occ.) But we say that passible man was so taken by God the Son, that His Deity remained impassible. Indeed the Son of God suffered, not by imputation but actually, all that Scripture testifies, in respect of that part of Him which could suffer, viz. in respect of the substance that He had taken on Him.

The Lord therefore sorrowed not from fear of suffering, for for this cause He had come that He should suffer, and had rebuked Peter for his fearfulness; (Matt. 14:31.) but for the wretched Judas, for the offence of the rest of the Apostles, for the rejection and reprobation of the Jewish nation, and the overthrow of unhappy Jerusalem.

Our Lord therefore sorrowed to prove the reality of the Man which He had taken upon Him; but that passion might bear no sway in His mind, He began to be sorrowful by pro-passion; for it is one thing to be sorrowful, and another to be very sorrowful.

He had accepted the disciples’ faith and the devotedness of their will, but He foresaw that they would be troubled and scattered abroad, and therefore bade them sit still in their places; for to sit belongs to one at ease, but they would be grievously troubled that they should have denied Him. In what fashion He went forward it describes, And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and very heavy; the same to whom He had shewn His glory in the mount.

By this place are overthrown the Manichæans, who said that He took an unreal body; and those also who said that He had not a real soul, but His Divinity in place of a soul

And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and heavy, or as Mark explains it, "he began to be afraid and heavy". Now these same disciples he had also taken up onto the mountain when he was to be transfigured, and to the daughter of Jairus the priest. And I ask whether perhaps he saw something more secret, in the time before he suffered, when Jesus, going to that place, wished to pray. For perhaps he saw standing near him "the kings of the earth and the princes" gathered "together against the Lord and against" him, "his Christ". And on this account, as though those many were set against him and mighty in wickedness, he began to be sorrowful and heavy, or even "to be afraid". And consider that he did not say: he was sorrowful and heavy, but: he began to be sorrowful and heavy. For there is a great difference between being sorrowful and beginning to be sorrowful. If therefore someone, in defense of human passions, brings forward to us that Jesus himself also was made sorrowful, let him hear that he who "was tempted in all things after our likeness, apart from sin", this one was not made sorrowful with the sorrow of that passion itself, but according to his human nature was brought only to the very beginning of sorrow and fear, that he might show to his disciples who were present (especially to Peter, who thought great things of himself) by these very facts what he also afterward said to them, that "the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak", and that one must never at any time trust in it but always be fearful concerning it; since incautious confidence leads to boastfulness, whereas fear of one's weakness exhorts us to flee to the help of God, just as it also urged the Lord himself to go forward a little and to fall on his face and to pray. Therefore he began indeed to be sorrowful and heavy according to his human nature, which is subject to such passions, but not according to his divine power, which is far removed from a passion of this kind.

And these things we say concerning Jesus, that you may not suppose, as certain heresies do, that he was a man, but that God took upon himself the true nature of a human body,

he who "was able to suffer together with our weaknesses", since he too was encompassed with the weak nature of a human body, "in like manner himself also partaking" of body and blood, since the children too (of whom he says: "behold, I and the children whom God has given me") "partake of flesh and blood". Seeing therefore the contest pressing upon him, which was for him not "against flesh and blood" but against so many "kings of the earth" standing near "and princes" gathered "together against" him as never before, he began "to be afraid" or to be sorrowful, suffering nothing more of sorrow or fear than only the beginning. For it is not written that he was afraid or was made sorrowful, but "he began to be afraid" and he began to be sorrowful, when he also said: my soul is sorrowful even unto death. This very thing seems to signify something of this sort, as if he were to say: sorrow has been begun in me, so that I am not altogether without a taste of sorrow; it is not always but only unto the time of death that it is in me, so that when I have died to sin, I may die also to all sorrow, of which there was in me only the beginning.
(ill. Luc. 22:43.) He is sorrowful, yet not Himself, but His soul; not His Wisdom, not His divine Substance, but His soul, for He took upon Him my soul, and my body.

(Fid. Orth. iii. 20.) Wherefore the passions of our nature were in Christ both by nature and beyond nature. By nature, because He left His flesh to suffer the things incidental to it; beyond nature, because these natural emotions did not in Him precede the will. For in Christ nothing befel of compulsion, but all was voluntary; with His will He hungered, with His will He feared, or was sorrowful. Here His sorrow is declared, Then saith he unto them, My soul is sorrowful even unto death.

He is sorrowful not because of death, but unto death, until He has set the Apostles free by His Passion. Let those who imagine Jesus to have taken an irrational soul, say how it is that He is thus sorrowful, and knows the season of His sorrow, for though the brute animals have sorrow, yet they know neither the causes of it, nor the time for which it must endure.

Or the sleep which He would have them forego is not bodily rest, for which at this critical time there was no room, but mental torpor, the sleep of unbelief.

Wait here, and watch with me; as if to say: although I told the other disciples, sit here, while I go over there to pray, and brought you three this far, I do not want you to advance further, for you are not yet able to. For this reason remain here watching, just as I too watch, knowing that I have indeed commanded the rest to sit there as those who are lesser, keeping them safe from this struggle, while I have brought you as those who are stronger, that "you may labor together with me in watchings and prayers". Yet you too remain here, so that each one may stand in the degree of his own calling, since even every grace (however great it may be) has also one above it. And that this is what he means when he says: remain here, is evident from what is said in what follows: but going forward a little he fell upon his face. Therefore let us remain where Jesus commands, according to what the Apostle also enjoins: "let each one, in whatever calling he was called, in this remain with God", so that we may do everything in order to watch together with him who "neither sleeps nor slumbers, keeping Israel". And he brought them to this, especially Peter who trusted greatly in himself, that they might see and hear where man's ability lies and how it is obtained. Let them indeed see him falling upon his face, and let them hear him saying: Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me, and let them learn not to be highminded about themselves but to esteem lowly things, and not to be swift to promise but careful to pray. Therefore he also led those who seemed more faithful and strong like Peter, in whom likewise boasting could easily find a place because of their confidence in their faith; but the ordinary ones (as far as the danger of boasting is concerned, I mean) are protected by that very smallness of their faith.

Or otherwise; My soul is sorrowful even unto death; as much as to say, Sorrow is begun in me, but not to endure for ever, but only till the hour of death; that when I shall die for sin, I shall die also to all sorrow, whose beginnings only are in me. Tarry ye here, and watch with me; as much as to say, The rest I bade sit yonder as weak, removing them from this struggle; but you I have brought hither as being stronger, that ye may toil with me in watching and prayer. But abide you here, that every man may stay in his own rank and station; since all grace, however great, has its superior.
"My soul," says He, "is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death; " and "the bread that I will give is my flesh, (which I will give) for the life of the world.

t: On the Resurrection of the Flesh
q: For He showed to what belongs (the incidents of) being destroyed, thrown down, and kept down-even to that to which it also appertains to be lifted and raised up again; although He was at the same time bearing about with Him "a soul that was trembling even unto death," but which did not fall through death, because even the Scripture informs us that "He spoke of His body.

He sometimes also fled from violence Himself, but for the same reason as had led Him to command the apostles to do so: that is, He wanted to fulfil His ministry of teaching; and when it was finished, I do not say He stood firm, but He had no desire even to get from His Father the aid of hosts of angels: finding fault, too, with Peter's sword. He likewise acknowledged, it is true, that His "soul was troubled, even unto death," and the flesh weak; with the design, (however,) first of all, that by having, as His own, trouble of soul and weakness of the flesh, He might show you that both the substances in Him were truly human; lest, as certain persons have now brought it in, you might be led to think either the flesh or the soul of Christ different from ours; and then, that, by an exhibition of their states, you might be convinced that they have no power at all of themselves without the spirit.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q:
However, even these He dismisses: "And He went on a little farther, and prayeth, saying, Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless not as I will, but as Thou wilt. And He cometh unto them, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, What, could ye not watch with me one hour? Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."

And He prays with earnestness, in order that the thing might not seem to be acting. And sweats flow over him for the same cause again, even that the heretics might not say this, that He acts the agony. Therefore there is a sweat like drops of blood, and an angel appeared strengthening Him, and a thousand sure signs of fear, lest any one should affirm the words to be feigned. For this cause also was this prayer. By saying then, "If it be possible, let it pass from me," He showed His humanity; but by saying, "Nevertheless not as I will, but as Thou wilt," He showed His virtue and self-command, teaching us even when nature pulls us back, to follow God. For since it was not enough for the foolish to show His face only, He uses words also. Again, words sufficed not alone, but deeds likewise were needed; these also He joins with the words, that even they who are in a high degree contentious may believe, that He both became man and died. For if, even when these things are so, this be still disbelieved by some, much more, if these had not been. See by how many things He shows the reality of the incarnation: by what He speaks, by what He suffers. After that He cometh and saith to Peter, as it is said, "What, couldest thou not watch one hour with me?" All were sleeping, and He rebukes Peter, hinting at him, in what He spake. And the words, "with me," are not employed without reason; it is as though He had said, Thou couldest not watch with me one hour, and wilt thou lay down thy life for me? and what follows also, intimates this self-same thing. For "Watch," saith He, "and pray not to enter into temptation." See how He is again instructing them not to be self-confident, but contrite in mind, and to be humble, and to refer all to God.

(de Cons. Ev. iii. 4.) And that none might think that He limited His Father's power, He said not, If thou canst do it, but If it may be, or, If it be possible; as much as to say, If thou wilt. For whatever God wills can be done, as Luke expresses more plainly; for he says not, If it be possible, but If thou wilt.

(in Ps. 32. enar. 2.) Christ thus as man shows a certain private human will, in which He who is our head figures both His own will and ours when He says, Let it pass from me. For this was His human will choosing something as apart for Himself. But because as man He would be righteous and guide Himself by God's will, He adds, Nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt; as much as to say to us, Man, behold thyself in Me, that thou canst will somewhat apart of thyself, and though God's will is other, this is permitted to human frailty.

(Quaest. Ev. i. 47.) Nor is that an absurd interpretation which makes Our Lord pray thrice because of the threefold temptation of His Passion. To the temptation of curiosity is opposed the fear of death; for as the one is a yearning for the knowledge of things, so the other is the fear of losing such knowledge. To the desire of honour or applause is opposed the dread of disgrace and insult. To the desire of pleasure is opposed the fear of pain.

Otherwise; He says not, Let this cup pass away from Me, for that would be the speech of one who feared it; but He prays that it may pass not so as that He should be passed over, but that when it has passed from Him, it may go to another. His whole fear then is for those who were to suffer, and therefore He prays for those who were to suffer after Him, saying, Let this cup pass from me, i. e. as it is drunk by Me, so let it be drunk by these, without mistrust, without sense of pain, without fear of death. He says, If it be possible, because flesh and blood shrink from these things, and it is hard for human bodies not to sink beneath their infliction. That He says, Not as I will, but as thou wilt, He would fain indeed that they should not suffer, lest their faith should fail in their sufferings, if indeed we might attain to the glory of our joint inheritance with Him without the hardship of sharing in His Passion. He says, Not as I will, but as thou wilt, because it is the Father's will that strength to drink of the cup should pass from Him to them, that the Devil might be vanquished not so much by Christ as by His disciples also.

Whence He says emphatically, This cup, that is, of this people of the Jews, who, if they shall put Me to death, can have no excuse for their ignorance, seeing they have the Law and the Prophets, who speak of Me.

And going forward a little he fell upon his face praying and saying: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me. He who said: "learn from me, for I am meek and lowly in heart", humbling himself in a praiseworthy manner, now also falls upon his face praying, and still more afterward humbles himself, "having become obedient unto death"; for the price of exaltation is humility, since indeed no one is exalted by God except him who shall have humbled himself for God's sake. And he falls upon his face praying having gone forward not much but a little from his three disciples who remained with him; for he did not wish to become far from them, but, stationed near them, to pray. And he who says, praying: if it be possible, let this cup pass from me, manifesting in his prayer his devotion, as a "beloved son" and one conforming to the dispositions of the Father, added: but not as I will, but as thou wilt, teaching that we should not pray that our own will be done but God's, whenever it happens that we will something other than God does. Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; but not as I will, but as thou wilt. Just as he began to be afraid and to be sorrowful, so according to that he also prays that the cup of the passion pass from him; but not as he himself wills, but as the Father wills. For taking upon himself the nature of human flesh, he fulfilled all its properties, so that he might not be thought to have had flesh in appearance, but in truth; according to which in this place he prays that the cup of the passion pass from him, but not as he himself wills, but as the Father wills: since it is proper to every faithful man, first indeed not to wish to suffer any pain, especially that which leads even unto death, because he is a man of flesh, but if God should so will, to acquiesce even against his own will, because he is faithful, lest he seem to despair in himself more than to hope in God. For just as we ought not to be over-confident, lest we seem to profess our own strength, so we ought not to act too faint-heartedly and to be distrustful, lest we seem to pronounce the powerlessness of God our helper. This will, therefore, which he speaks: if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; but not as I will, but as thou wilt, is not according to his divine and impassible substance, but according to his human and weak nature. But another interpretation of this place is such: that, as the "son of the love" of God, according to his foreknowledge indeed he loved those who from among the Gentiles were going to believe; but the Jews, as the seed of the holy fathers, "whose is the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the promises", he loved as branches of the good olive tree. And loving them he saw what things they were going to suffer, seeking him unto death and choosing Barabbas unto life; therefore, grieving over them, he said: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; and again recalling his desire and seeing how great a benefit of the whole world was going to come about through his passion, he said: but not as I will, but as thou wilt. He saw still that on account of that cup of the passion even Judas, who was one of the twelve, would be a son of perdition; and again he understood that through that cup of the passion the principalities and powers were to be triumphed over in his body. On account of these, therefore, whom in his passion he did not wish to perish, he said: Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; but on account of the salvation of the whole human race, which through his death was to be gained for God, he said, as if reconsidering: but not as I will, but as thou wilt, that is: if it be possible, that without my passion all those good things may come forth which are to come forth through my passion, let this passion pass from me, so that both the world may be saved and the Jews may not perish in my passion. But if without the perdition of certain many the salvation cannot be brought in, as pertains to thy justice, let it not pass as I will, but as thou wilt. As if he should say: this indeed is my will, but since thy will is far more eminent (as of the unbegotten God, as of the Father of all), for this reason I rather will thy will to be done than mine.

But this cup of the passion which is drunk Scripture names in many places, especially that which is properly drunk by the martyrs, as it is there: "what shall I render to the Lord for all the things which he has rendered to me? I will receive the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord". If therefore the cup of salvation is the cup of martyrdom, it is necessary that we preserve that cup, drinking the whole of it, because it is the cup of salvation, so that we pour out nothing of it. He therefore drinks the whole cup who suffers for the testimony whatever shall have been brought upon him; but he pours it out as he receives it who, called to martyrdom, denies lest he suffer anything. There is also another kind of "inebriating cup", which one drinks after he shall have eaten the "table" prepared for him by God "against those who trouble" the just man.

But it is to be noted that Mark indeed and Luke wrote this very thing, who also set forth Jesus as tempted by the devil; but John indeed sets forth the passion in the same manner as the others, yet does not bring in Jesus praying that the cup might pass from him, just as neither does he set forth Jesus as tempted by the devil. And I judge this to be the reason: that these indeed set forth concerning him more according to his human nature than according to the divine, but John more according to the divine than according to the human (for this reason, because according to the human nature he was tempted, but the divinity was untemptable). Therefore three evangelists indeed set forth him as tempted, but John, according to what he had begun: "in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word", knows not that God the Word can be tempted. So also here these three indeed reported that Jesus asked of the Father that the cup might pass from him, since it was also proper to man (so far as pertains to the weakness of the flesh) to wish to escape the passion, but John, having as his purpose to set forth Jesus as God the Word, knowing that he himself is "the life and the resurrection", knows not that the impassible God flees from the passion.

He took with Him the self-confident Peter, and the others, that they might see Him falling on His face and praying, and might learn not to think great things, but little things of themselves, and not to be hasty in promising, but careful in prayer. And therefore, He went forward a little, not to go far from them, but that He might be near them in His prayer. Also, He who had said above, Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart, now commendably humbling Himself, falls on His face. But He shows His devotion in His prayer, and as beloved and well-pleasing to His Father, He adds, Not as I will, but as thou wilt, teaching us that we should pray, not that our own will, but that God's will, should be done. And as He began to have fear and sorrow, He prays accordingly that the cup of His Passion may pass from Him, yet not as He wills, but as His Father wills; wills, that is, not according to His Divine and impassible Substance, but according to His human and weak nature. For in taking upon Him the nature of human flesh, He fulfilled all the properties thereof, that it might be seen that He had flesh not in appearance only, but in-reality. The believer indeed must in the first instance be loth to incur pain, seeing it leads to death, and he is a man of flesh; but if it be God's will, he acquiesces because he is a believer. For as we ought not to be too confident that we may not seem to make a boast of our own strength; so neither ought we to be distrustful, lest we should seem to charge God our helper with weakness. It is to be observed that Mark and Luke write the same, but John does not introduce this prayer of Jesus', that this cup may pass from Him, because the first three are rather occupied about Him, according to His human nature, John according to His divine. Otherwise; Jesus makes this petition, because He sees what the Jews will suffer for requiring His death.

Then again considering the benefit that would accrue to the whole world from His Passion, He says, But not as I will, but as thou wilt; i. e. If it be possible for all these benefits which shall result from My Passion to be procured without it, let it pass from Me, and both the world be saved, and the Jews not be condemned in putting Me to death. But if the salvation of many cannot be procured without the destruction of a few, saving Thy justice, let it not pass away. Scripture, in many places, speaks of passion as a cup that is drained; and it is drained by him, who in testimony suffers whatever is inflicted upon him. He sheds it, on the contrary, who denies in order to avoid suffering.

And for this reason He puts first "the willing spirit," that, looking to the natures respectively of both the substances, you may see that you have in you the spirit's strength as well as the flesh's weakness; and even from this may learn what to do, and by what means to do it, and what to bring under what,-the weak, namely, under the strong, that you may not, as is now your fashion, make excuses on the ground of the weakness of the flesh, forsooth, but put out of sight the strength of the spirit. He also asked of His Father, that if it might be, the cup of suffering should pass from Him. So ask you the like favour; but as He did, holding your position,-merely offering supplication, and adding, too, the other words: "but not what I will, but what Thou wilt.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: Not without reason doth He inveigh against Peter most, although the others also had slept; but to make him feel by this also, for the cause which I mentioned before. Then because the others also said the same thing (for when Peter had said (these are the words), "Though I must die with Thee, I will not deny Thee; likewise also," it is added, "said all the disciples"); He addresses Himself to all, convicting their weakness. For they who are desiring to die with Him, were not then able so much as to sorrow with Him wakefully, but sleep overcame them.

When then He returned to His disciples and found them sleeping, He rebukes Peter, Could ye not watch one hour with me? He addresses Peter rather than the rest, because he had most loudly boasted that he would not be offended.
Or the sleep which He would have them forego is not bodily rest, for which at this critical time there was no room, but mental torpor, the sleep of unbelief.
And though Jesus went but a little forward, they could not watch one hour in His absence; let us therefore pray that Jesus may never depart even a little from us.

And he came to his disciples and found them sleeping, and he says to Peter: so you were not able to keep watch with me for one hour? Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation (26, 40. 41).

As long indeed as Jesus was present with his disciples they did not sleep, but when he had gone forward a little from them they could not keep watch for even one hour in his absence. For which reason let us pray that Jesus may never at any time go forward even a little from us, but may fulfill in us what he promised, saying: "behold, I will be with you all the days even to the consummation of the age". For thus we shall keep watch, as he shakes off sleep from our soul, without which it is not possible to fulfill the commandment that says: "give not sleep to your eyes, nor slumber to your eyelids, that you may escape like a roe from the nets and like a bird from the snare". Yet, coming to the disciples and finding them sleeping, he rouses them by his word to hear, so that now, as though to those hearing, he may say what he says: so you were not able to keep watch with me for one hour. And he commands them to watch, so that watching we may pray. And he watches who does good works, he watches who acts carefully concerning the truth of the faith, lest he fall into some dark doctrine. For he who thus watches and prays, his prayer is heard; for this is what he signifies when he says: watch and pray, namely that first we should watch and thus, watching, pray. that you may not enter into temptation: this (according to what many understand) is such as if he were to say: that you may not be tempted; but if it so please God, submit to God, just as you heard me praying. But consider whether it is possible to understand it rather in this way, since our very life "is a temptation" according to Job; and to enter into temptation or to come into temptation is to fall into temptation and to be overcome by it. And I think that no one comes to Jesus and into temptation at the same time; but if indeed he comes to Jesus, he does not come into temptation, but if he comes into temptation, he does not come to Jesus. For no one comes to Jesus except him whom the Father draws to Jesus, that he may be raised up by him. Therefore we come to Jesus, so that even if the tempter has pursued us and evils have come from him, we may not be seized by them, as it is written: "evils shall pursue you and shall not overtake you". But to the sinner it is said, correspondingly: "evils shall pursue you and shall overtake you".

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: And at one time He addresses Himself to Peter, at another to all in common. And to him He saith, "Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat; but I have prayed for thee;" and to all in common, "Pray that ye enter not into temptation;" every way plucking up their self-will, and making them earnest-minded. Then, that He might not seem to make His language altogether condemnatory, He saith, "The spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak." For even although thou dost desire to despise death, yet thou wilt not be able, until God stretch forth His hand, for the carnal mind draws down.

"Pray that you do not enter into temptation"—that you enter not again into "contentions, envying, animosities, dissension, detractions, seditions, whispering." For we have not planted and watered the Lord's garden in you only to reap these thorns from you. But if your weakness still stirs up a storm, pray that you may be delivered from temptation. Those among you who trouble you, whoever they may be, will incur judgment unless they amend their lives.
And why He thus encouraged them to pray that they might not enter into temptation, He adds, For the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak; this He says not of Himself, but addresses them.

It is impossible that the human mind should not be tempted, therefore He says not Watch and pray that ye be not tempted, but that ye enter not into temptation, that is, that temptation vanquish you not.

This is against those rash persons who think that whatever they believe they can perform. The more confident we are of our zeal, the more mistrustful should we be of the frailty of the flesh.
Otherwise; In these words He shows that He took real flesh of the Virgin, and had a real soul, saying that His spirit is willing to suffer, but His flesh weak in fearing the pain of Passion.

Finding them thus sleeping, He rouses them with a word to hearken, and commands them to watch; Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation; that first we should watch, and so watching pray. He watches who does good works, and is careful that He does not run into any dark doctrine, for so the prayer of the watchful is heard.

Here it should be enquired, whether as all men's flesh is weak, so all men's spirit is willing, or whether only that of the saints; and whether in unbelievers the spirit is not also dull, as the flesh is weak. In another sense the flesh of those only is weak whose spirit is willing, and who with their willing spirit do mortify the deeds of the flesh. These then He would have watch and pray that they should not enter into temptation, for the more spiritual any one may be, the more careful should he be that his goodness should not suffer a great fall.

The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak, just as your spirit too, O Peter, was willing to make a promise, but your flesh will be weak when it comes to confessing. But this must be considered: whether just as the flesh of all human beings is weak, so the spirit of all is willing, or whether, though the flesh of all human beings is indeed weak, yet the spirit of all human beings is not willing, but only that of the saints. Therefore it is to the apostles alone, or to those who are found to be like them, that he says, the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak; but of unbelievers both the spirit is sluggish and the flesh is weak. If, then, it holds that Christ says this only to the saints, he prompts us to inquire, since there is a weak flesh also in another sense — yet only of those whose spirit is willing. For I say that the flesh is weak of that man who has no sin nor a strong wisdom of the flesh but a defective one, who with a willing spirit has mortified the "works of the flesh" and reduced the wisdom of the flesh to nothing, so that he may "always carry about the death of Christ in his body", the spirit evidently prevailing in its desires against the desires of the flesh, since "the flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh". And "these" things in the imperfect indeed "are opposed to one another", but in the perfect the flesh no longer opposes, but has been mortified, and the wisdom of the flesh has been weakened in the flesh, and its desire has been extinguished; but in it the wisdom of the spirit lives, lives and works. Of which weakness the Lord too says to the apostle, that "strength is made perfect in weakness", that is, in the weakness of the flesh and of its wisdom. On account of which the Apostle says: "for when I am weak, then am I strong"; for then each one of us becomes strong, when his own flesh has been weakened, so that it does not accomplish the "works of the flesh", but the strength of Christ dwells in it. Whence he said: "so I fight, indeed", and "I chastise my body and bring it into servitude", since by many chastisements a man makes his flesh weak, advancing in spirit and mortifying the "works of the flesh". This, then, is what he wishes to say to his disciples according to that tradition: "watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation" — you whose spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak; for he who is more spiritual and more perfect ought to be the more anxious, lest his great good have a grievous fall.

Would any man have dared to touch even with his little finger, the body of Christ, if it had been of an unusual nature; or to smear His face with spitting, if it had not invited it (by its abjectness)? Why talk of a heavenly flesh, when you have no grounds to offer us for your celestial theory? Why deny it to be earthy, when you have the best of reasons for knowing it to be earthy? He hungered under the devil's temptation; He thirsted with the woman of Samaria; He wept over Lazarus; He trembles at death (for "the flesh," as He says, "is weak " ); at last, He pours out His blood.

To us it is matter for thankfulness if we do now publicly confess our iniquities or our turpitudes: for we do at the same time both make satisfaction for our former sins, by mortification of our flesh and spirit, and lay beforehand the foundation of defences against the temptations which will closely follow. "Watch and pray," saith (the Lord), "lest ye fall into temptation." And the reason, I believe, why they were tempted was, that they fell asleep; so that they deserted the Lord when apprehended, and he who continued to stand by Him, and used the sword, even denied Him thrice: for withal the word had gone before, that "no one untempted should attain the celestial kingdoms.

This passage He confirms by subsequent ones, saying, "Pray that ye be not tempted; " yet they were tempted, (as they showed) by de-setting their Lord, because they had given way rather to sleep than prayer.
From the saying of our Lord we know that the flesh is weak, the spirit willing. Let us not, withal, take delusive comfort from the Lord's acknowledgment of the weakness of the flesh.

If the "spirit is willing, but the flesh," without patience, "weak," where, save in patience, is the safety of the spirit, and of the flesh itself? But when the Lord says this about the flesh, pronouncing it "weak," He shows what need there is of strengthening, it-that is by patience-to meet every preparation for subverting or punishing faith; that it may bear with all constancy stripes, fire, cross, beasts, sword; all which prophets and apostles, by enduring, conquered!
But we read "that the flesh is weak; " and hence we soothe ourselves in some cases.
But we read "that the flesh is weak; " and hence we soothe ourselves in some cases. Yet we read, too, that "the spirit is strong; " for each clause occurs in one and the same sentence.

And how long will this most shameless "infirmity" persevere in waging a war of extermination against the "better things? "The time for its indulgence was (the interval) until the Paraclete began His operations, to whose coming were deferred by the Lord (the things) which in H's day "could not be endured; "which it is now no longer competent for any one to be unable to endure, seeing that He through whom the power of enduring is granted is not wanting. How long shall we allege "the flesh," because the Lord said, "the flesh is weak? " But He has withal premised that "the Spirit is prompt," in order that the Spirit may vanquish the flesh-that the weak may yield to the stronger.

He likewise acknowledged, it is true, that His "soul was troubled, even unto death," and the flesh weak; with the design, (however,) first of all, that by having, as His own, trouble of soul and weakness of the flesh, He might show you that both the substances in Him were truly human; lest, as certain persons have now brought it in, you might be led to think either the flesh or the soul of Christ different from ours; and then, that, by an exhibition of their states, you might be convinced that they have no power at all of themselves without the spirit. And for this reason He puts first "the willing spirit," that, looking to the natures respectively of both the substances, you may see that you have in you the spirit's strength as well as the flesh's weakness; and even from this may learn what to do, and by what means to do it, and what to bring under what,-the weak, namely, under the strong, that you may not, as is now your fashion, make excuses on the ground of the weakness of the flesh, forsooth, but put out of sight the strength of the spirit.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: And again He prayed in the same way, saying, "Father, if this cannot pass from me except I drink it, Thy will be done," showing here, that He fully harmonizes with God's will, and that we must always follow this, and seek after it.

That He prays for this a second and a third time, comes of the feelings belonging to human frailty, through which also He feared death, thus giving assurance that He was truly made man. For in Scripture when any thing is repeated a second and third time, that is the greatest proof of its truth and reality; as, for example, when Joseph says to Pharaoh, And for that thou sawedst it twice, it is proof of the thing being established by God. (Gen. 41:32.)

Otherwise, He bare in His own body all the infirmities of us His disciples who should suffer, and nailed to His cross all wherein we are distressed; and therefore that cup cannot pass from Him, unless He drink it, because we cannot suffer, except by His passion.

Or otherwise; He prays a second time that if Nineveh, or the Gentile world, cannot be saved unless the gourd, i. e. the Jews, be withered, His Father's will may be done, which is not contrary to the Son's will, who Himself speaks by the Prophet, I am content to do thy will, O God. (Ps. 40:8.)

(Serm. 58, 5.) This speech of the Head is the health of the whole body, this saying is instruction to the faithful, animates the confessor, crowns the martyr. For who could vanquish the hatred of the world, or the whirlwind of temptations, or the terrors of the persecutors, if Christ did not in all and for all say to the Father, Thy will be done. Let all the sons of the Church then utter this prayer, that when the pressure of some mighty temptation lies upon them, they may embrace endurance of the suffering, disregarding its terrors.

There were, I conclude, two ways in which this cup of Passion might pass from the Lord. If He should drink it, it would pass away from Him, and afterwards from the whole race of mankind also; if He should not drink it, it would perhaps pass from Him, but from men it would not pass. He would fain therefore that it should so pass from Him as that He should not at all taste its bitterness, yet only if it were possible, saving the righteousness of God. If it were not possible, He was rather willing to drink it, that so it might pass from Him, and from the whole race of mankind rather than against His Father's will shun the drinking thereof.

Again going away, Jesus prayed, saying: My Father, if this cannot pass from me unless I drink it, let your will be done.

Now, however, he asks that the cup pass from him, and if not in that way—as he himself had willed—that it pass in the way the Father wills. Here now we shall expound according to what we are able to understand, so that together with this we may seem to have expounded also what precedes. For I judge that that cup of the passion was indeed altogether going to pass from Jesus, but with a difference: namely, that if he should drink it, it would afterward pass both from himself and from the whole race of men; but if he should not drink it, it would perhaps pass from himself, yet would not pass from men, but would remain with them until it should bring them to completion. This cup of the passion, therefore, he wished principally to pass from him in such a way that he should not taste its bitterness at all, if indeed this were possible as regards the justice of God. For when he said "if it is possible" he was not referring to the power of God alone but also to his justice: since as regards the power of God all things are possible, whether just or unjust, but as regards his justice—for he is not only powerful but also just—not all things are possible, but those alone which are just. But if it could not come to pass, he preferred that he should drink it and so it should pass from him and from the whole race of men, rather than that he should act against the Father's will by shunning the drinking of it. Therefore, for the sake of the good outcome that was to follow after the bitterness of the cup was drunk, he prays a second time, saying: My Father, if it is not possible for it to pass unless I drink it, let your will be done.

It is clear, then, that he wished to drink it. For by comparison it was better that it should pass because of his drinking of it than that it should not pass because he had not drunk it. For suppose the Lord had not drunk that cup and for this reason it had not passed from him: without doubt neither would the spirits working sins have passed from the human race, and fittingly neither would the penalties have passed which were owed for the sins. Therefore it was expedient for all that the cup should pass from him, because the Savior drank it, so that all of us who believe in him who drank it may not drink that cup "of unmixed wine", which gives to drink and is going to give to drink to "all the nations", so that those drinking it "may become drunk and vomit, and cease to rage". For just as "he died for us all", so that the death hostile to Christ might pass us by, so for us all (who were "debtors", bound to drink forever) he drank that cup, so that by this very thing—that the cup passes from him—it might pass also from us who do not drink it. Concerning this cup Jeremiah says: "The Lord God of Israel said to me: Take this cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you, and they shall drink and vomit and cease to rage before the sword which I send into the midst of them". Those, therefore, who hear the Lord and live according to his word and are cleansed through faith in him, no longer have need of that cleansing which comes about through that cup of wrath. For just as those who have been washed have no need to be washed, because they are clean (because they are Christ's disciples), so those who are not clean have need of that cup, the Lord exhorting them: "Drink and be drunk and vomit". For hear how Jeremiah speaks (or rather God in Jeremiah), exhorting those who have need of such a cup, since they ought willingly to drink it who have need of such a cleansing. And since God says these things exhorting them to drink, consider what he says further below: "And it shall be", he says, "when they are unwilling to receive the cup from your hand to drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: Drinking you shall drink, for in the city upon which my name has been invoked, upon it I will begin to bring evils, and you shall be cleansed with cleansing".

But observe that after the first prayer "he came to the disciples and found them sleeping", and likewise after the second coming he found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy—but I think not so much the eyes of their bodies as of their souls. For as yet he had not removed from the eyes of his disciples the burden laid upon them, "for he had not yet been glorified". And just as "the Holy Spirit was not yet, because Jesus had not yet been glorified", so their eyes had not yet been unveiled from the burden "because Jesus had not yet been glorified". Whence he does not rebuke them, but going away again a third time he prayed the same thing, teaching us also through this very thing, that we should not fail in prayer but should persevere in that very word of prayer, until we obtain those things which we have already begun to ask.
Christ singly prays for all, as He singly suffers for all. Their eyes were heavy, i. e. an oppression and stupefaction came on as their denial drew near.
And I suppose that the eyes of their body were not so much affected as the eyes of their mind, because the Spirit was not yet given them.
He prayed the third time, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might be established.
Or, He prays thrice for the Apostles, and for Peter in particular, who was to deny Him thrice.
Wherefore He does not rebuke them, but goes again and prays, teaching us that we should not faint but should persevere in prayer, until we obtain what we have begun to ask.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q:
"And He came and found them asleep." For besides that it was late at night, their eyes also were weighed down by their despondency. And the third time He went and spake the same thing, establishing the fact, that He was become man. For the second and third time is in the Scriptures especially indicative of truth; like as Joseph also said to Pharaoh, "Did the dream appear to thee the second time? For truth was this done, and that thou mightest be assured that this shall surely be." Therefore He too once, and twice, and three times spake the same thing, for the sake of proving the incarnation.

And wherefore came He the second time? In order to reprove them, for that they were so drowned in despondency, as not to have any sense even of His presence. He did not however reprove them, but stood apart from them a little, showing their unspeakable weakness, that not even when they had been rebuked, were they able to endure. But He doth not awake and rebuke them again, lest He should smite them that were already smitten, but He went away and prayed, and when He is come back again, He saith, "Sleep on now, and take your rest." And yet then there was need to be wakeful, but to show that they will not bear so much as the sight of the dangers, but will be put to flight and desert Him from their terror, and that He hath no need of their succor, and that He must by all means be delivered up, "Sleep on now," He saith, "and take your rest; behold the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners."

He shows again that what is done belongs to a divine dispensation.

But He doth not this only, but also, by saying, "into the hands of sinners," He cheers up their minds, showing it was the effect of their wickedness, not of His being liable to any charge.

"Rise, let us be going; behold, he is at hand that doth betray me." For by all means He taught them, that the matter was not of necessity, nor of weakness, but of some secret dispensation. For, as we see, He foreknew that Judas would come, and so far from flying, He even went to meet him.

(de Cons. Ev. iii. 4.) This speech as Matthew has it seems self-contradictory. For how could He say, Sleep on, and take your rest, and immediately continue, Rise, let us be going. This contradiction some have endeavoured to reconcile by supposing the words, Sleep on, and take your rest, to be an ironical rebuke, and not a permission; it might be rightly so taken if need were. But as Mark records it, when He had said, Sleep on, and take your rest, He added, it is enough, and then continued, The hour is come, behold, the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners; (Mark 14:41.) we clearly understand the Lord to have been silent some time after He had said, Sleep on, to allow of their doing so, and then after some interval to have roused them with, Behold, the hour is at hand. And as Mark fills up the sense with, it is enough, that is, ye have had rest enough.

After His persevering prayer, after His departures and several returns, He takes away their fear, restores their confidence, and exhorts them to sleep on, and take their rest.

Or, He bids them sleep on, and take their rest, because He now confidently awaited His Father's will concerning the disciples, concerning which He had said, Thy will be done, and in obedience to which He drunk the cup that was to pass from Him to us, diverting upon Himself the weakness of our body, the terrors of dismay, and even the pains of death itself.

And whereas, when He returned and found them sleeping, He rebukes them the first time, the second time says nothing, the third time bids them take their rest; the interpretation of this is, that at the first after His resurrection, when He finds them dispersed, distrustful, and timorous, He rebukes them; the second time, when their eyes were heavy to look upon the liberty of the Gospel, He visited them, sending them the Spirit, the Paraclete; for, held back by attachment to the Law, they slumbered in respect of faith; but the third time, when He shall come in His glory, He shall restore them to quietness and confidence.

Having concluded His third prayer, and having obtained that the Apostles' terror should be corrected by subsequent penitence, He goes forth undaunted by the prospect of His own Passion to meet His pursuers, and offers Himself voluntarily to be sacrificed. Arise, let us be going; as much as to say, Let them not find you trembling, let us go forth willingly to death, that they may see us confident and rejoicing in suffering; Lo, he that shall betray me draweth near.
Or, He prays thrice for the Apostles, and for Peter in particular, who was to deny Him thrice.

Or, the sleep He now bids His disciples take is of a different sort from that which is related above to have befallen them. Then He found them sleeping, not taking repose, but because their eyes were heavy, but now they are not merely to sleep, but to take their rest, that this order may be rightly observed, namely, that we first watch with prayer that we enter not into temptation, and afterwards sleep and take our rest, when having found a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob, (Ps. 132:3.) we may go up into our bed, and give sleep to our eyes. It may be also that the soul, unable to sustain a continual energy by reason of its union with the flesh, may blamelessly admit some relaxations, which may be the moral interpretation of slumbers, and then again after due time be quickened to new energy.

And then, coming, he said to his disciples: sleep now and rest; behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be handed over into the hands of sinners. Rise, let us go; behold, he who will betray me has drawn near (26, 45. 46). Then — without doubt after the third prayer. But that sleep, which he now orders his disciples to sleep, is not the same as the one that is written above to have twice befallen the disciples. For there he "found them sleeping" but not also resting, and "again he found them sleeping" with their eyes weighed down; but now he commands them not simply to sleep, but with rest. For to sleep and rest according to the command of Christ differs greatly from a sleeping against the will of him who says: "remain here and keep watch with me" and who reproaches them on account of their sleep and says: "so, could you not watch one hour with me?" Therefore he did not say things contrary to himself when he said there: "watch with me", and here: sleep and rest, but so that the order might be preserved: that first indeed we should watch, praying that we may not enter into temptation, and afterward that we should sleep and rest according to Christ's command.

Which sleep Solomon too sets down in a promise to those who live well, saying in his Proverbs: "for if you sit down, you will be without fear; but if you sleep, you will sleep sweetly, and you will not fear a terror that comes upon you nor the assaults of the impious rushing in". And David, knowing the diverse watchings and sleepings, "swore to the Lord and vowed a vow to the God of Jacob": not to go up onto the couch of his bed nor to give sleep to his eyes nor slumber to his eyelids, and to do this for so long, until he should find "a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob", so that when he has found a place for the Lord, he may go up onto the couch of his bed and give sleep to his eyes as they renew themselves and, after rest, prepare themselves for a new and more divine rising up, according to what is wont to happen to bodily men after natural and healthy sleep. But perhaps also the soul, not being able always to bear labors inasmuch as it is created and incarnate and not sufficient to preserve the good without interruption, will obtain relaxations without any blame, which morally are called sleeps and slumbers, so that, having relaxation up to some little space of time, it may rise renewed and be raised again. But whether this will be forever or not, let him who is able inquire more abundantly concerning such things — both to inquire and to understand from the divine Scriptures and to declare it without danger.

Behold, the hour has drawn near, and the Son of Man will be betrayed into the hands of sinners. On account of this hour, I think, he also said to his mother: "My hour has not yet come". For here too he teaches that the approaching hour was bringing this about, that the Son of Man should be betrayed into the hands of sinners. Would that Jesus had then been betrayed into the hands of those sinners only! But as it is, I think that Jesus is always betrayed into the hands of sinners, whenever those who seem to believe in Jesus have Jesus in their hands while being sinners. But also, as often as a righteous man who has Jesus within himself is brought into the power of sinners who do to him what they can, Jesus is betrayed into the hands of sinners.

When He had roused them from sleep, seeing in the Spirit Judas drawing near to betray Him, though the disciples could not yet see him, He says, Behold, the hour is at hand, and the Son of man is betrayed into the hands of sinners.

And even now Jesus is betrayed into the hands of sinners, when those who seem to believe in Jesus, continue to sin while they have Him in their hands. Also whenever a righteous man, who has Jesus in Him, is put into the power of sinners, Jesus is delivered into the hands of sinners.

He says not, Draws near to thee, for indeed the traitor was not near Him, but had removed himself far off through his sins.

Rise, let us go; behold, he who will betray me has drawn near. After he had roused them from that sleep of which we have spoken, he consequently says to his disciples: Rise, let us go. And seeing in the spirit Judas approaching for the betrayal, who was not yet visible to his disciples, he says: Behold, he who will betray me has drawn near. But I think that behold, he has drawn near to me and behold, he who will betray me has drawn near are not one and the same thing; for his betrayer was not drawing near to Jesus himself (he who had removed himself far from Jesus by his sins and by the giving-up by which he had resolved to betray him), but he had drawn near to betraying the Son of God, whom he had already given up. But indeed all transgressors first give up Jesus, and afterwards betray him.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q: At any rate, "While He yet spake, lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and elders of the people." Seemly surely are the instruments of the priests! "with swords and staves" do they come against Him! And Judas, it is said, with them, one of the twelve. Again he calleth him "of the twelve," and is not ashamed. Now he that betrayed Him gave them a sign, saying, "Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is He, hold Him fast." Oh! what depravity had the traitor's soul received. For with what kind of eyes did he then look at his Master? with what mouth did he kiss Him? Oh! accursed purpose; what did he devise? What did he dare? What sort of sign of betrayal did he give? Whomsoever I shall kiss, he saith. He was emboldened by his Master's gentleness, which more than all was sufficient to shame him, and to deprive him of all excuse for that he was betraying one so meek.

One of the twelve, by association of name, not of desert. This shows the monstrous wickedness of the man who from the dignity of the Apostleship became the traitor. To show that it was out of envy that they seized Him, it is added, A great multitude sent by the Chief Priests and elders of the people.

And while he was still speaking, behold, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, sent from the chief priests and the elders of the people. But someone will also ask the reason why a great crowd was gathered with swords and clubs against him; and this great crowd was, according to John, a cohort of soldiers and attendants dispatched by the chief priests. And someone may say that, because of the multitude of those from among the people who had already believed in him, they came against him in such numbers, fearing lest the great multitude of believers should snatch him out of their hands. But I think there was also another reason for the multitude gathered against him: that those who supposed he was accustomed to cast out demons by Beelzebul imagined that by certain sorcerous and magical arts he could escape from the midst of those wishing to hold him. And perhaps some of them had heard how once, when he was already about to be hurled down from the brow of the mountain, he escaped the hands of those already holding him, not by a simple and human flight but by some other means beyond human nature. For this very reason also, in Mark, Judas said to the crowd that was coming with him with swords and clubs: "whomever I shall have kissed, that is he; hold him and lead him away carefully"; for in saying "lead him away carefully" he seems to have spoken maliciously and with a hidden meaning, as if to say: unless you hold him carefully and lead him away, he will escape you when he wishes. And they, hearing this according to Judas's estimation—as though it were not by his Father's divinity that he was helped to do this or many other things—did everything so as to hold and guard him carefully. There are many now also who wage war against Jesus with spiritual swords of malignant spirits and likewise with clubs, just as those men did; over whose snares Jesus becomes altogether superior, although for a time he takes their assaults upon himself, that the sins of those plotting against him may be filled up and the malice of their will against the truth of the only-begotten Word of God may be made manifest. And those who thus wage war against Jesus with swords and clubs, coming with various and diverse doctrines about God, lie in wait for Jesus deliberately. But there are also those who, dispatched by the elders of their own impious people, wage war against the word of truth, which is in Jesus.

Some may say that a great multitude came, because of the great multitude of those who already believed, who, they feared, might rescue Him out of their hands; but I think there is another reason for this, and that is, that they who thought that He cast out dæmons through Beelzebub, supposed that by some magic He might escape the hands of those who sought to hold Him.
Or, because whenever they had hitherto attempted to seize Him, He had escaped them they knew not how; as also He might then have done had He been so minded.

Even now do many fight against Jesus with spiritual weapons, to wit, with divers and shifting dogmas concerning God. It deserves enquiry why, when He was known by face to all who dwelt in Judæa, he should have given them a sign, as though they were unacquainted with His person. But a tradition to this effect has come down to us, that not only had He two different forms, one under which He appeared to men, the other into which He was transfigured before His disciples in the mount, but also that He appeared to each man in such degree as the beholder was worthy; in like manner as we read of the manna, that it had a flavour adapted to every variety of use, and as the word of God shows not alike to all. They required therefore a sign by reason of this His transfiguration.

But the one who betrayed him gave them a sign, saying: whomever I shall kiss, that is he, hold him fast. And immediately approaching Jesus he said: hail Rabbi, and he kissed him. But Jesus said to him: friend, to what have you come?

It is worth inquiring for what cause, when Jesus had taught openly through every city and village and synagogue, preaching the word of the Gospel (so that his fame went out into the whole region), and had been made manifest in his face to all who dwelt in Judaea, Judas gave to those sent by the chief priests a sign, as though they did not recognize his likeness, saying: whomever I shall kiss, that is he. But that even those who had come with Judas to seize him had frequently seen him is made manifest from this, that Jesus himself says to the crowds: you have come out to seize me as though against a robber, with swords and clubs: daily I was sitting with you in the temple teaching, and you did not hold me. Similarly John also reports that he said: I have spoken openly to this world; I always taught in the synagogue and in the temple, where all the Jews come together.

Now such a tradition has come to us concerning him: that there were not only two forms in him (one indeed according to which all saw him, but the other according to which he was transfigured before his disciples on the mountain, when also his face shone as the sun), but that he also appeared to each one according as that one had been worthy. And though he was himself, he seemed to all as though not himself, according to what is written concerning the manna, when God "sent bread from heaven to the sons of Israel, having every delight and suited to every taste", when "complying with the desire of the one who offered it, it was turned into whatever anyone had wished". And this tradition does not seem to me to be incredible, whether bodily on account of Jesus himself, that he might be seen by men in one manner and another, or on account of the very nature of the Word, which does not appear alike to all. But if this is so, it is possible to find the solution of that which is inquired. For although the crowds coming with Judas frequently saw him, nonetheless they had need (on account of his transformations) of one who would point him out to them, one having a more intimate knowledge of him through much dwelling with him, so that he might understand his transformations according to which he was accustomed to appear to his own. This same thing is signified also through John the Evangelist, where "Jesus, knowing the things that were to come upon him, going forth outside said: whom do you seek? And they said: Jesus the Nazarene. And he said to them: I am he" and "they went back and fell backward". You see that they did not recognize him, though they had frequently seen him, on account of his transfigurations.

But if anyone should also inquire into that cause, why Judas betrayed Jesus "with a kiss", we will give this reason: that, according to some indeed, he wished to preserve a certain reverence toward his master, not daring to rush upon him openly and shamelessly to profess himself the betrayer of his master. But according to others Judas did this for this reason, fearing lest perhaps, if he had shown himself openly an adversary and betrayer of his master, he himself might become for him a cause of escape, since he could (as far as pertained to Judas's own opinion) by certain more secret disciplines flee away and make himself small. Therefore, that Jesus, suspecting nothing of the kind (according to what Judas supposed) but thinking him a friend (he knows not how), might thus be seized unexpectedly, for this reason he gave this sign, not now knowing that if he had been unwilling to be seized, he never would have been seized, but that willingly he offered himself to the hands of sinners. But I think that all betrayers of the truth also, feigning to love the truth and using the sign of a kiss as though by a certain token of charity, betray the word of God to its adversaries who wish to hold him, adversaries clothed with nothing peaceful, but having warlike swords and injuries and clubs. And the betrayer says to Jesus: Rabbi; for all heretics, just as Judas, so say to Jesus: Rabbi, who also kiss him just as Judas did. To all of whom Jesus speaks placable words, though they are all Judas the betrayer: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" And he says to him, reproaching him for the pretense of his friendship: friend, to what have you come?

For by this name we know no one of the good called in the Scriptures. For to the wicked man, and one not clothed with the wedding garments, he says: "friend, why have you come in here not having a wedding garment?" And he is wicked who also hears in the parable of the denarius: "friend, I do you no wrong; did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours, and go; but I wish to give also to this last one just as to you also".

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 83
q:
But wherefore doth He say this? Because often when seized by them He had gone out through the midst, without their knowing it. Nevertheless, then also this would have been done, if it had not been His own will that He should be taken. It was at least with a view to teach them this, that He then blinded their eyes, and Himself asked, "Whom seek ye?" And they knew Him not, though being with lanterns and torches, and having Judas with them. Afterwards, as they had said, "Jesus;" He saith, "I am He" whom ye seek: and here again, "Friend, wherefore art thou come?"

For after having shown His own strength, then at once He yielded Himself. But John saith, that even to the very moment He continued to reprove him, saying, "Judas, betrayest thou the Son of Man with a kiss?" Art thou not ashamed even of the form of the betrayal? saith He. Nevertheless, forasmuch as not even this checked him, He submitted to be kissed, and gave Himself up willingly; and they laid their hands on Him, and seized Him that night on which they ate the passover, to such a degree did they boil with rage, and were mad. However, they would have had no strength, unless He had Himself suffered it. Yet this delivers not Judas from intolerable punishment, but even more exceedingly condemns him, for that though he had received such proof of His power, and lenity, and meekness, and gentleness, he became fiercer than any wild beast.

If it be asked why Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss, according to some it was because He desired to keep up the reverence due to his Master, and did not dare to make an open assault upon Him; according to others, it was out of fear that if he came as an avowed enemy, he might be the cause of His escape, which he believed Jesus had it in His power to effect. But I think that all betrayers of truth love to assume the guise of truth, and to use the sign of a kiss. Like Judas also, all heretics call Jesus Rabbi, and receive from Him mild answer.
