(non occ.) He says, Wherefore art thou come? as much as to say, Thy kiss is a snare for Me; I know wherefore thou art come; thou feignest thyself My friend, being indeed My betrayer.

Or, after Friend, for what thou art come, that do, is understood. Then came they, and laid their hands on Jesus, and held him. Then, that is, when He suffered them, for ofttimes they would have done it, but were not able.

Then they came and laid hands on Jesus and held him fast.

After the kiss, those crowds at once, delaying nothing, perhaps fearing lest Jesus escape from their hands, laid hands on him. And behold, one of those who were with Jesus, stretching out his hand, drew his sword, and striking the servant of the high priest, cut off his ear. Now one of those who were with Jesus, not yet clearly grasping within himself that evangelical patience handed down to him by Christ, nor the peace which he gave to his disciples, but acting according to the power granted to the Jews through the law concerning enemies, stretching out his hand took up the sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. And as John says: "… and cut off his right ear", in whom the servant's name is also given, for he was called "Malchus". And perhaps what Peter was doing was a mystery. For the right hearing of the Jewish people was to be cut off on account of their malice displayed against Jesus. For even though they seem to hear the law, they now hear with a left hearing the shadow of the tradition about the law, not the truth, since they are servants of the word that professes the service of God, yet does not serve in truth. The mystery of this word was against Christ … the adversary of Christ, the high priest Caiaphas. And it seems to me that, since all those who have believed from among the Gentiles, being established as one people in Christ, by this very fact that they believed in Christ became the cause that the right hearing of the Jews should be cut off, according to what had been prophesied concerning them: "Make heavy the ears of this people, and press down their eyes, lest seeing they see and hearing they understand and be converted, and I heal them".

And Jesus said unto him, Friend, wherefore art thou come? He says, Friend, upbraiding his hypocrisy; for in Scripture we never find this term of address used to any of the good, but as above, Friend, how camest thou in hither? (Matt. 22:12.) and, Friend, I do thee no wrong. (Matt. 20:13.)

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
Who was this "one," who cut off the ear? John saith that it was Peter. For the act was of his fervor.

But this other point is worth inquiry, wherefore they were bearing swords? For that they bore them is evident not hence only, but from their saying when asked, "here are two." But wherefore did Christ even permit them to have swords? For Luke affirms this too, that He said unto them, "When I sent you without purse, and scrip, and shoes, lacked ye anything?" And when they said, "Nothing," He said unto them, "But now, he that hath a purse, let him take it, and a scrip, and he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment, and buy one." And when they said, "Here are two swords," He said unto them, "It is enough."

Wherefore then did He suffer them to have them? To assure them that He was to be betrayed. Therefore He saith unto them, "Let him buy a sword," not that they should arm themselves, far from it; but by this, indicating His being betrayed.

And wherefore doth He mention a scrip also? He was teaching them henceforth to be sober, and wakeful, and to use much diligence on their own part. For at the beginning He cherished them (as being inexperienced) with much putting forth of His power but afterwards bringing them forth as young birds out of the nest, He commands them to use their own wings. Then, that they might not suppose that it was for weakness He is letting them alone, in commanding them also to work their part, He reminds them of the former things, saying, "When I sent you without purse, lacked ye anything?" that by both they might learn His power, both wherein He protected them, and wherein He now leaveth them to themselves by degrees.

But whence were the swords there? They were come forth from the supper, and from the table. It was likely also there should be swords because of the lamb, and that the disciples, hearing that certain were coming forth against Him, took them for defense, as meaning to fight in behalf of their Master, which was of their thought only. Wherefore also Peter is rebuked for using it, and with a severe threat. For he was resisting the servant who came, warmly indeed, yet not defending himself, but doing this in behalf of his Master.

Christ however suffered not any harm to ensue. For He healed him, and showed forth a great miracle, enough to indicate at once both His forbearance and His power, and the affection and meekness of His disciple. For then he acted from affection, now with dutifulness. For when he heard, "Put up thy sword into its sheath," he obeyed straightway, and afterwards nowhere doeth this.

Otherwise; The ear of the High Priest's servant is cut off by the Apostle, that is, Christ's disciple cuts off the disobedient hearing of a people which were the slaves of the Priesthood, the ear which had refused to hear is cut off so that it is no longer capable of hearing.

In another Gospel, (John 18:10.) Peter is represented as having done this, and with his usual hastiness; and that the servant's name was Malchus, and that the ear was the right ear. In passing we may say, that Malchus, i. e. one who should have been king of the Jews, was made the slave of the ungodliness and the greediness of the Priests, and lost his right ear so that he might hear only the worthlessness of the letter in his left.

For though they seem even now to hear the Law, yet is it only with the left ear that they hear the shadow of a tradition concerning the Law, and not the truth. The people of the Gentiles is signified by Peter; for by believing in Christ, they become the cause of cutting off the Jews' right ear.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
But another saith, that they moreover asked, "Shall we smite?" but that He forbad it, and healed the man, and rebuked His disciple, and threatened, that He might move him to obedience. "For all they that take the sword," He said, "shall die with the sword."

And he adds a reason, saying, "Think ye that I cannot pray to my Father, and He shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels? But that the Scriptures might be fulfilled." By these words He quenched their anger, indicating that to the Scriptures also, this seemed good. Wherefore there too He prayed, that they might take meekly what befell Him, when they had learnt that this again is done according to God's will.

And by these two things, He comforted them, both by the punishment of them that are plotting against Him, "For all they," He saith, "that take the sword shall perish with the sword;" and by His not undergoing these things against His will, "For I can pray, He saith, "to my Father."

And wherefore did He not say, "Think ye that I cannot destroy them all?" Because He was more likely to be believed in saying what He did say; for not yet had they the right belief concerning Him. And a little while before He had said, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful even unto death," and, "Father, let the cup pass from me;" and He had appeared in an agony and sweating, and strengthened by an angel.

Since then He had shown forth many tokens of human nature, He did not seem likely to speak so as to be believed, if He had said, "Think ye that I cannot destroy them." Therefore He saith, "What, think ye that I cannot pray to my Father?" And again He speaks it humbly, in saying, "He will presently give me twelve legions of angels." For if one angel slew one hundred and eighty-five armed thousands, what need of twelve legions against a thousand men? But He frames His language with a view to their terror and weakness, for indeed they were dead with fear. Wherefore also He brings against them the Scriptures, saying, "How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled?" alarming them by this also. For if this be approved by the Scriptures, do ye oppose and fight against them?

(cont. Faust. xxvii. 70.) That is, every one who uses the sword. And he uses the sword, who, without the command or sanction of any superior, or legitimate authority, arms himself against man's life. For truly the Lord had given commandment to His disciples to take the sword, but not to smite with the sword. Was it then at all unbeseeming that Peter after this sin should become ruler of the Church, as Moses after smiting the Egyptian was made ruler and chief of the Synagogue? For both transgressed the rule not through hardened ferocity, but through a warmth of spirit capable of good; both through hatred of the injustice of others; both sinned through love, the one for his brother, the other for his Lord, though a carnal love.

But all who use the sword do not perish by the sword; of those who have used the sword either judicially, or in self-defence against robbers, fever or accident carries off the greater part. Though if according to this every one who uses the sword shall perish by the sword, justly was the sword now drawn against those who were using the same for the promotion of crime.
The Lord then bids him return his sword into its sheath, because He would destroy them by no weapon of man, but by the sword of His mouth.
With what sword then shall he perish, that takes the sword? By that fiery sword which waves before the gate of paradise, and that sword of the Spirit which is described in the armour of God.

(Serm. 22.) The Lord of the zealous Apostle will not suffer his pious feeling to proceed further, Then saith Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place. For it was contrary to the sacrament of our redemption that He, who had come to die for all, should refuse to be apprehended. He gives therefore licence to their fury against Him, lest by putting off the triumph of His glorious Cross, the dominion of the Devil should be made longer, and the captivity of men more enduring.
Otherwise; Every one who uses the sword to put man to death perishes first by the sword of his own wickedness.

Then Jesus said to him: turn your sword back into its place.

At once Jesus says to the man who had used the sword and had cut off the right ear of that servant, not: draw out the sword, but: turn the sword back into its place. There is therefore some place belonging to the sword, from which it is not permitted to take it up by one who does not wish to perish, above all by the sword. For Jesus wishes his disciples to be peaceable, so that, laying down this warlike sword, they may take up another, peaceable sword, which Scripture calls "the sword of the spirit". And it seems to me like what he says: all who take up the sword, shall also perish by the sword, that is, all who are not peaceable but stirrers-up of war shall perish in that war which they stir up, so that in them the sword is the mystery of war and strife. And I think that all the turbulent and the instigators of wars and those who disturb the souls of men, above all the souls of the churches, take up the sword by which they too shall perish; since "he who digs a pit shall himself fall into it", since their "pain shall be turned back upon" their own "head", and their "iniquity shall come down upon" their "brain". But also, hearing simply what he says, those who take up the sword shall perish by the sword, it befits us to beware, lest on the occasion of military service or of avenging our own injuries we draw out the sword, or on any occasion whatever — all of which this evangelical teaching of Christ abominates, commanding us to fulfill what is written: "with those who hated peace I was peaceable". If therefore with those who hate peace we ought to be peaceable, against no one ought we to use the sword.

Thus, wishing (speaking to one who had not learned) to teach us all that willingly "he handed himself over for us all", he adds and says: or do you think that I cannot now ask my Father, and he will furnish me more than twelve legions of angels? as though he were saying: you indeed have thus drawn the sword and struck the ruler's servant, as if rendering help to me, but I, if I had wished, could by asking the Father obtain help not human but of better beings, that is, of angels, and not of one but of more than twelve legions. From this it is shown that, according to the likeness of the legions of worldly warfare, there are also legions of angels of the heavenly warfare, warring against the legions of the demons dwelling in the tombs. For in Luke too "a multitude of the heavenly host" was heard "praising God" on account of Christ's nativity. But if "there was a multitude of the heavenly host praising God", and all warfare is understood to be established on account of adversaries, consequently that host too wars for God on account of adversaries. But Jacob also called a certain place the "camp" of the Lord, since he beheld there the warfare of angels; and wherever there are those who fear God, around them are the camps of angels; for "the angel of the Lord shall send [a host] round about those who fear him and shall deliver them", as the book of Kingdoms relates was the case also around Elisha.

And note: do you think it was as though inferior to the angels, or needing the help of angels, that the Savior said: or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will furnish me more than twelve legions of angels? — or was it perhaps according to the estimation of Peter, who wished to bring him help and brought forth the sword and cut off the servant's ear, that he spoke such things? For rather do the angels have need of the help of the only-begotten Son of God than he of theirs. For this reason, that which is written, "for he shall give his angels charge concerning you, to keep you in all your ways", is understood to be said not of the only-begotten Son of God, but either in the person of Christ concerning every just man, whom Christ was bearing in his body, or concerning Christ according to his human nature. And finally, that which he says, he will deliver you "from ruin and the noonday demon", in no way befits the Son of God; but also what he says, "you shall not fear the terror of the night, the arrow that flies by day, the trouble that walks about in the darkness", befits a just man rather than the Son of God. Since therefore he could receive the legions, he was unwilling to receive them, so that through his patience the Scriptures prophesying about him might be fulfilled, since it befitted him thus to suffer.

But how will a Christian man war, nay, how will he serve even in peace, without a sword, which the Lord has taken away? For albeit soldiers had come unto John, and had received the formula of their rule; albeit, likewise, a centurion had believed; still the Lord afterward, in disarming Peter, unbelted every soldier. No dress is lawful among us, if assigned to any unlawful action.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
And wherefore did He not say, "Think ye that I cannot destroy them all?" Because He was more likely to be believed in saying what He did say; for not yet had they the right belief concerning Him. And a little while before He had said, "My soul is exceeding sorrowful even unto death," and, "Father, let the cup pass from me;" and He had appeared in an agony and sweating, and strengthened by an angel.

Since then He had shown forth many tokens of human nature, He did not seem likely to speak so as to be believed, if He had said, "Think ye that I cannot destroy them." Therefore He saith, "What, think ye that I cannot pray to my Father?" And again He speaks it humbly, in saying, "He will presently give me twelve legions of angels." For if one angel slew one hundred and eighty-five armed thousands, what need of twelve legions against a thousand men? But He frames His language with a view to their terror and weakness, for indeed they were dead with fear. Wherefore also He brings against them the Scriptures, saying, "How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled?" alarming them by this also. For if this be approved by the Scriptures, do ye oppose and fight against them?

That is to say, I need not the aid of the Apostles, though all the twelve should fight for me, seeing I could have twelve legions of the Angelic army. The complement of a legion among the ancients was six thousand men; twelve legions then are seventy-two thousand Angels, being as many as the divisions of the human race and languaget.

We might also understand by the Angels the Roman armies, for with Titus and Vespasian all languages had risen against Judæa, and that was fulfilled, The whole world shall fight for him against those foolish men. (Wisd. 5:21.)

This shows that the armies of heaven have divisions into legions like earthly armies, in the warfare of the Angels against the legions of the daemons. This He said not as though He needed the aid of the Angels, but speaking in accordance with the supposition of Peter, who sought to give Him assistance. Truly the Angels have more need of the help of the Only-begotten Son of God, than He of theirs.
He has power to ask, if He will, legions of angels from the Father for His help. He exclaims that God had forsaken Him.
And He quiets their fears not thus only, but by reference to Scripture, How then shall the Scriptures he fulfilled that thus it must be?
This speech shows a mind willing to suffer; vainly would the Prophets have prophesied truly, unless the Lord asserts their truth by His suffering.

They did not lay hands on Him in the temple because they feared the multitude, therefore also the Lord went forth that He might give them place and opportunity to take Him. This then teaches them, that if He had not suffered them of His own free choice, they would never have had strength to take Him. Then the Evangelist assigns the reason why the Lord was willing to be taken, adding, All this was done that the Scriptures of the Prophets might be fulfilled.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
And to His disciples He saith these things; but to the others, "Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me? I sat daily teaching in the temple, and ye laid no hold on me."

See how many things He doeth that might awaken them. He cast them to the ground, He healed the servant's ear, He threatened them with being slain; "For they shall perish with the sword," He saith, "who take the sword." By the healing of the ear, He gave assurance of these things also; from every quarter, both from the things present, and from the things to come, manifesting His power, and showing that it was not a work of their strength to seize Him. Wherefore He also adds, "I was daily with you, and sat teaching, and ye laid no hold on me;" by this also making it manifest, that the seizure was of His permission. He passed over the miracles, and mentions the teaching, that He might not seem to boast.

When I taught, ye laid no hold on me; when I held my peace, did ye come against me? I was in the temple, and no one seized me, and now do ye come upon me late and at midnight with swords and staves? What need was there of these weapons against Him, who was with you always? by these things teaching them, that unless He had voluntarily yielded, not even then would they have succeeded. For neither could they (who were not able to hold Him when in their hands, and who, when they had got Him in the midst of them, had not prevailed) even then have succeeded, unless He had been willing.
It is folly then to seek with swords and staves Him who offers Himself to your hands, and with a traitor to hunt out, as though lurking under cover of night, one who is daily teaching in the temple.
As much as to say, Robbers assault and study concealment; I have injured no one, but have healed many, and have ever taught in your synagogues.

Having commanded Peter to put up his sword, which was an instance of patience, and having (as another Evangelist writes [Luke 22:51.]) healed the ear that was cut off, which was an instance of the greatest mercy, and of Divine power, it now follows, In that hour said Jesus to the multitudes, to the end that if they could not remember His past goodness, they might at least confess His present,) Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me?

In that hour Jesus said to the crowds: Have you come out to seize me as against a robber, with swords and clubs? Daily I sat among you in the temple teaching, and you did not lay hold of me.

The sense of what is said in this passage seems to me to be as follows, that the Savior says to the crowds: If anyone wishes to seize a robber, it is not incongruous to come to him with swords and clubs, because such is the robber, that he dares all things provided he suffer nothing bad, and if he can he is rather ready both to use the sword and the club against those who wish to seize him, than of his own accord to hand himself over into their hands. But I, since I am not such, all who are in Judea know it—some indeed seeing my teaching and my works, but others having heard about me or following my manner of life; for daily sitting in the holy place of the temple (as though a fitting place for divine teachings) I made plain the things that pertained to piety and to a sound life according to the law of God, and through this I commended myself as one who is peaceable. But that neither your plotting against me nor your soldiery mounted with swords and clubs has any suitable reason, is manifest to all who know me. But how is it that you were not even satisfied, seeing daily my continuance in the temple of God and myself offering myself to all who wished to hear me, that I might join them to myself for their profit through word and life unto the blessedness of God—or that then indeed you did not lay hold of me when you saw me teaching and doing nothing worthy of blame, but now you reckon me as though changed, so that you suppose I ought to be seized as though a robber? But neither in this do you find any occasion, as though I had changed with respect to the word from those things which I had first set forth, wishing to profit by words and deeds. And observe: after he had said to Peter: "Put back your sword into its sheath" (which is the mark of patience), after he had restored the severed ear, as another evangelist relates (which had been at once a token of the highest kindness and likewise of divine power), then he spoke these words, so that they might appear trustworthy from the preceding words and deeds, so that even if they do not remember past good deeds, they might at least recognize the present ones.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
After this, He solves also the difficulty why He willed it then. For, "this was done," He saith, "that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled." See how even up to the last hour, and in the very act of being betrayed, He did all things for their amendment, healing, prophesying, threatening. "For," He saith, "they shall perish by the sword." To show that He is suffering voluntarily, He saith, "I was daily with you teaching;" to manifest His accordance with the Father, He adds, "That the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled."

But wherefore did they not lay hold on Him in the temple? Because they would not have dared in the temple, on account of the people. Wherefore also He went forth without, both by the place and by the time giving them security, and even to the last hour taking away their excuse. For He who, in order that He might obey the prophets, gave up even Himself, how did He teach things contrary to them?

"Then all His disciples," it is said, "forsook Him, and fled." For when He was seized, they remained; but when He had said these things to the multitudes, they fled. For thenceforth they saw that escape was no longer possible, when He was giving Himself up to them voluntarily, and saying, that this was done according to the Scriptures.
They pierced my hands and my feet; (Ps. 22:16.) and in another place, He is led as a sheep to the slaughter; (Is. 53:7, 8.) and, By the iniquities of my people was He led to death.

For because all the Prophets had foretold Christ's Passion, he does not cite any particular place, but says generally that the prophecies of all the Prophets were being fulfilled.

In this act is shown the Apostles' frailty; in the first ardour of their faith they had promised to die with Him, but in their fear they forgot their promise and fled. The same we may see in those who undertake to do great things for the love of God, but fail to fulfil what they undertake; they ought not to despair, but to rise again with the Apostles, and recover themselves by penitence.

Now all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Concerning matters of this kind … but it is a great task now to select from the prophets what sort of sayings of the prophets those are which were then fulfilled, when Christ said that he would suffer these things; and it belongs to a diligent man, and to one who knows much, to gather together the words of the prophets which have been fulfilled. And in the hundred and eighth Psalm [109] perhaps you will find very many things agreeing with these, concerning those who came with Judas to arrest Jesus, just as other things concerning Judas were said in the same Psalm. then they all forsook him and fled together. Fearing, therefore, the crowds and their leader Judas, they fled. For they did not yet have the Spirit, "because Jesus had not yet been glorified," and the "spirit" "of power and of love"; and if they had had it, they would not have been weakened, nor would they have done anything else apart from divine love.

On the other hand, Christ, who spoke not guile from His mouth, and who exhibited all righteousness and humility, not only (as we have above recorded it predicted of Him) was not exposed to that kind of death for his own deserts, but (was so exposed) in order that what was predicted by the prophets as destined to come upon Him through your means might be fulfilled; just as, in the Psalms, the Spirit Himself of Christ was already singing, saying, "They were repaying me evil for good; " and, "What I had not seized I was then paying in full; " They exterminated my hands and feet; " and, "They put into my drink gall, and in my thirst they slaked me with vinegar; " "Upon my vesture they did cast (the) lot; " just as the other (outrages) which you were to commit on Him were foretold,-all which He, actually and thoroughly suffering, suffered not for any evil action of His own, but "that the Scriptures from the mouth of the prophets might be fulfilled."

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
And when these were fled, "they lead Him away to Caiaphas; but Peter followed, and entered in to see what the end should be."

Great was the fervor of the disciple; neither did he fly when he saw them flying, but stood his ground, and went in with Him. And if John did so too, yet he was "known to the high priest."

And why did they lead Him away there where they were all assembled? That they might do all things with consent of the chief priests. For he was then high priest, and all were waiting for Christ there, to such a degree did they spend the whole night, and give up their sleep for this object. For neither did they then eat the passover, but watched for this other purpose. For John, when he had said that "it was early," added, "they entered into the judgment hall, lest they should be defiled, but that they might eat the passover."

What must we say then? That they ate it on another day, and broke the law, on account of their eager desire about this murder. For Christ would not have transgressed as to the time of the passover, but they who were daring all things, and trampling under foot a thousand laws. For since they were exceedingly boiling with rage, and having often attempted to seize Him, had not been able; having then taken Him unexpectedly, they chose even to pass by the passover, for the sake of satiating their murderous lust.

Wherefore also they were all assembled together, and it was a council of pestilent men, and they ask some questions, wishing to invest this plot with the appearance of a court of justice. For "neither did their testimonies agree together;" so feigned was the court of justice, and all things full of confusion and disorder.

(Cons. Ev. iii. 6.) They that had laid hold on Jesus led Him away to Caiaphas the High Priest. But He was first taken to Annas, father-in-law to Caiaphas, as John relates. And He was taken bound, there being with that multitude a tribune and cohort, as John also records. (John 18:12.)

But Josephus writesu, that this Caiaphas had purchased the priesthood of a single year, notwithstanding that Moses, at God's command, had directed that High Priests should succeed hereditarily, and that in the Priests likewise succession by birth should be followed up. No wonder then that an unrighteous High Priest should judge unrighteously.

But they, having seized Jesus, led him away to Caiaphas the chief priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered together.

For I think that the word of the Jewish servitude, in which those now abandoned profess to serve, is Caiaphas, who wars against the truth of Jesus, who is called the chief priest; but Jesus according to the truth is the priest, the Word of God, under whom are set all those who serve God the Father acceptably. But where Caiaphas is chief priest, there the scribes are gathered together, that is, the lettered men who preside over the letter that kills. And according to the quality of the scribes are also the elders, who recline not upon the truth but upon the oldness of the bare letter, and who wish to transact nothing further.

Where Caiaphas the High Priest is, there are assembled the Scribes, that is, the men of the letter, who preside over the letter that killeth; and Elders, not in truth, but in the obsolete ancientness of the letter.

Great was the zeal of Peter, who fled not when He saw the others fly, but remained, and entered in. For though John also went in, yet he was known to the Chief Priest. He followed afar off, because he was about to deny his Lord.
(Quaest. Ev. i. 46.) And also that the Church should follow, i. e. imitate, the Lord's Passion, but with great difference. For the Church suffers for itself, but Christ for the Church.
He went in, either out of the attachment of a disciple, or natural curiosity, seeking to know what sentence the High Priest would pass, whether death, or scourging.
For had he kept close to his Lord's side, he could never have denied Him. This also shows that Peter should follow his Lord's Passion, that is, imitate it.
Peter followed Him afar off, He would neither keep close to Him, nor altogether leave Him, but followed afar off.

Now Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the chief priest, and having gone inside he was sitting with the servants to see the outcome of the matter.

Now while the master was being led away, Peter indeed was following, yet he could not follow him from close at hand, but from afar off, neither departing from him altogether nor walking along with him, nor beside him but following at a distance he came to the courtyard of the chief priest. And having gone inside, Peter was sitting within, neither ministering according to what those servants did nor doing the things which Jesus had taught, but he was awaiting the outcome of all these things, wishing to see it, since as yet he did not understand nor see the outcome of Christ's dispensations, toward what they were tending. For their outcome is not in the courtyard of Caiaphas, nor where "the scribes and elders" of that people are gathered together. If, however, one should look properly at the outcome, he will see the very Word of God and the Wisdom saying: "I am A and Ω, the beginning and the end".

When the Chief Priests were thus assembled, this conventicle of ruffians sought to give their conspiracy the character of a legal trial. But it was entirely a scene of confusion and uproar, as what follows shows, Though many false witnesses came, yet found they none.

False witnesses have place when there is any good colour for their testimony. But no pretext was found which could further their falsehoods against Jesus; notwithstanding there were many desirous to do a favour to the Chief Priests. This then is a great testimony in favour of Jesus, that He had lived and taught so irreproachably, that though they were many, and crafty, and wicked, they could find no semblance of fault in Him.

Now the chief priest and the elders and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus, that they might deliver him to death, and they found none; and many false witnesses came forward, and they found none (26, 59. 60ᵃ).

And through these things it is made manifest that Jesus "did no sin, nor was there guile in his mouth". But that his life was most pure and altogether beyond reproach, taking away the occasions of those who seek occasions, is demonstrated from this: that his adversaries found not what they might say against him or give a semblance of truth (yet all the priests and the whole council sought it, and could find nothing plausible); for false testimonies then have their place when they are brought forward with some semblance of truth, but against Jesus not even a semblance was found that could lend aid to lies against Jesus — and this, though there were many willing to grant a favor to Caiaphas and the chief priests and the scribes and the elders and the whole council, which desired to hear this very thing. And those who consider these things render the greatest praise to Jesus on account of his life and his teaching, who so blamelessly both said and did all things, that they found in him no plausible ground for reproach — neither the wicked, nor the many, nor those so cunning and clever.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q: "But false witnesses came, and said, This fellow said, I will destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it." And indeed He had said, "In three days," but He said not, "I will destroy," but, "Destroy," and not about that temple but about His own body.

But at last there came forward two false witnesses and said: This man said: I am able to destroy the temple of God and after three days to rebuild it (26, 60ᵇ. 61).

Do not suppose that Matthew called these two witnesses false without cause, since their testimonies seemed to be true from the fact that John sets forth that Christ said: "Destroy this temple, and I in three days will raise it up", when there is also added: "But this he said concerning the temple of his body".

But observe the cunning of the two false witnesses, by what persuasion they, taking their start from a certain true saying which Jesus had spoken, fabricated a false testimony. For Jesus did not say: I destroy this temple, and in three days I raise it up, but: "Destroy … this temple, and in three days I will raise it up".

But the false witnesses reported that he had said what had not been said by him, nor did he say: I am able to destroy the temple of God and in three days to rebuild it. Therefore he did not himself promise to do the impiety of destroying the temple, but he committed it to those who were fit for such a work, saying: "Destroy this temple". But what did he reserve for himself, namely: "And I in three days will raise it up".

And the fact that "he said this concerning the temple of his body" the Jews, hindered by their malice, misheard and understood concerning that temple of stone,

which is manifest from the fact that, answering, they said: "In forty and six years was this temple built, and dost thou raise it up in three days?" And consider that not one false witness came forward for this testimony (for one was not sufficient for those wishing to kill Jesus, since the law commanded: "One witness shall not stand to give testimony against a man"), but neither were there three; for though many false witnesses came forward, scarcely two were found who seemed to say anything. But neither were their testimonies in agreement, as Mark sets forth; for he says in this manner, that "the chief priests and the whole council sought testimony against Jesus, that they might deliver him to death, and found none; for many spoke false testimony against him, and their testimonies were not in agreement. And others rising up spoke false testimony against him: that we heard him saying: that I destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days I will make another not made with hands. But neither so were their testimonies in agreement". For a testimony is in agreement when they say the same things, but they are not in agreement when they are dissonant with one another, such as were the testimonies of these who were bringing forward testimonies against Jesus. And if Matthew and Mark speak the truth (which we ought to believe), let us attempt to show how not even the testimonies of these two themselves were in agreement, since they did not bring forward the same things. For according to Matthew they said: This man said: I am able to destroy the temple of God and in three days to rebuild it, but according to Mark: "That we heard him saying: that I destroy this temple made with hands, and in three days I will rebuild another not made with hands". Whether therefore, saying these things twice, since they did not say the same things, their testimonies were not found in agreement with one another; or whether the one said what Matthew sets forth, and the other what Mark wrote, and thereby "their testimonies were not in agreement" with one another.

At last came two false witnesses. How are they false witnesses, when they repeat only what we read that the Lord spoke? A false witness is one who takes what is said in a different sense from that in which it was said. Now this the Lord had spoken of the temple of His Body, and they cavil at His expressions, and by a slight change and addition produce a plausible charge. The Lord's words were, Destroy this temple; (John 2:19.) this they make into, I can destroy the Temple of God. He said, Destroy, not 'I will destroy,' because it is unlawful to lay hands on ourselves. Also they phrased it, And build it again, making it apply to the temple of the Jews; but the Lord had said, And I will raise it up again, thus clearly pointing out a living and breathing temple. For to build again, and to raise again, are two different things.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
What then doth the high priest? Willing to press Him to a defense, that by that he might take Him, he saith, "Hearest Thou not what these witness against Thee? But He held His peace."

For the attempts at defense were unprofitable, no man hearing. For this was a show only of a court of justice, but in truth an onset of robbers, assailing Him without cause, as in a cave, or on a road.

Wherefore "He held His peace," but the other continued, saying, "I adjure Thee by the living God, that Thou tell us whether Thou be the Christ, the Son of the living God. But He said, Thou hast said. Nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds. Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy." And this he did to add force to the accusation, and to aggravate what He said, by the act. For since what had been said moved the hearers to fear, what they did about Stephen, stopping their ears, this high priest doth here also.

And yet what kind of blasphemy was this? For indeed before He had said, when they were gathered together, "The Lord said unto my Lord. Sit Thou on my right hand," and interpreted the saying, and they dared say nothing, but held their peace, and from that time forth gainsaid Him no more. Why then did they now call the saying a blasphemy? And wherefore also did Christ thus answer them? To take away all their excuse, because unto the last day He taught that He was Christ, and that He sitteth at the right hand of the Father, and that He will come again to judge the world, which was the language of one manifesting His full accordance with the Father.

Headlong and uncontrolled rage, unable to find even a false accusation, moves the High Priest from his throne, the motion of his body showing the emotion of his mind. And the High Priest arose, and said unto him, Answerest thou nothing to the things which these witness against Thee?

For as God, He knew that whatever He said would be twisted into an accusation against Him. But at this His silence before false witnesses and ungodly Priests, the High Priest was exasperated, and summons Him to answer, that from anything He says he may raise a charge against Him.

And the chief priest, rising up, said to him: Do you answer nothing to the things which these men testify against you? But Jesus was silent (26, 62. 63a).

In these events one may understand as fulfilled the prophecy which says: "while the sinner stood against me, I was made dumb and was humbled and kept silent from good things", so that that sinner foretold in these words may be understood to be Caiaphas, who stood against Jesus. At the same time we learn also from this passage to despise the voices of slanderers and false witnesses, so that we neither hold them worthy of our reply, nor defend our own selves where the things said against us are not consistent. For what need is there to resist those who resist themselves by saying things contrary to themselves? Especially where it is a greater thing freely and bravely to be silent than to defend oneself without any profit, so that we may not be humbled by false witnesses and wicked slanderers.

And the chief priest said to him: I adjure you by the living God, that you tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God. And Jesus said to him: You have said it (26, 63ᵇ. 64ᵃ).

And indeed in the Law we find the practice of adjuring used on several occasions. For in Numbers the Law says that "the priest shall adjure her" (that is, that woman in whose husband there has arisen "a spirit of jealousy"), "and shall say to the woman" (this is, the priest): "if no one has lain with you, and unless you have transgressed so as to be defiled by a man not your own, you shall be innocent of this cursed water of accusation". And after a few words: "and the priest", he says, "shall adjure the woman with the adjurations of this curse". Likewise in the third book of Kingdoms king Ahab says to Micaiah: "Yet twice more do I adjure you, that you speak to me the truth in the name of the Lord". Now the king adjured the prophet, and he adjured not as the priest in Numbers; for the latter did so from the precept of the Law, but the former of his own choice. And now in the present passage the priest adjures Jesus by the living God. But I judge that it is not fitting for a man who wishes to live according to the Gospel to adjure another. For it is similar to what the Lord himself says in the Gospel: "But I say, not to swear at all" and not to adjure at all;

for if it is not permitted to swear, so far as concerns the evangelical commandment of Christ, it is true that neither is it permitted to adjure another.

Therefore it is manifest that the chief priest unlawfully adjured Jesus, although he may seem to have adjured him by the living God.

Someone will ask whether it is fitting even to adjure demons. And he who looks to the many who have dared to do such things will say that this is not done without reason; but he who looks to Jesus … commanding the demons, but also giving power to his disciples over all demons

and to heal infirmities, will say that to adjure demons is not according to the power given by the Savior: for it is a Jewish practice. This (even if sometimes something of the kind is done by our own people) is similar to that whereby demons are wont to be adjured by the adjurations written by Solomon. But those very people who use those adjurations sometimes do not even use properly established books, and with certain adjurations received even from the Hebrew they adjure the demons.

Nevertheless it was not fitting for our Lord to answer the adjuration of the chief priest, as though he had suffered compulsion from the one adjuring against his own will. For which reason he neither denied that he was the Christ, the Son of God, nor openly confessed it, but as though taking the very one adjuring him as witness (since it is he himself who in the priest's questioning was pronounced the Christ, the Son of God), saying: You have said it.

And since "everyone who commits sin is born of the devil", and the chief priest was committing sin by plotting against Jesus, therefore he was born of the devil, and as one born of the devil he was imitating his own father, who twice, in doubt, questions the Savior: "if you are the Son of God", as is written in his temptations; for "if you are the Son of God" and if you are the Christ, the Son of God are alike. For in this passage one may rightly say that to doubt concerning the Son of God whether he himself be the Christ is the work of the devil and of the chief priest plotting against our Lord. But Peter was not found to be such; for without any doubt he pronounced: "you are the Christ, the Son of the living God", nor did he there place if. For which reason he was called "blessed", because "not flesh and blood" had revealed it to him, "but God the Father who is in heaven". But those who say with doubt: "if you are the Son of God", are strangers to all blessedness. For because that chief priest was not worthy of the teaching of Christ, therefore he does not teach him, nor say, "I am", but taking the word of his own mouth he turns it into a refutation of him, saying: You have said it, so that in this way he might seem to be refuted, not taught.

This place teaches us to contemn the clamours of slanderers and false witnesses, and not to consider those who speak unbeseeming things of us worthy of an answer; but then, above all, when it is greater to be manfully and resolutely silent, than to plead our cause in vain.

Under the Law, we do indeed find many instances of this adjuration (Numb. 5:19, 1 Kings 22:16.); but I judge that a man who would live according to the Gospel should not adjure another; for if we are not permitted to swear, surely not to adjure. But he that regards Jesus commanding the daemons, and giving His disciples power over them, will say, that to address the daemons by the power given by the Saviour, is not to adjure them. But the High Priest did sin in laying a snare for Jesus; imitating his father, who twice asked the Saviour, If thou be Christ the Son of God. (Matt. 4.) Hence one might rightly say, that to doubt concerning the Son of God, whether Christ be He, is the work of the Devil.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
"But He said, Thou hast said. Nevertheless I say unto you, Hereafter shall ye see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds. Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy." And this he did to add force to the accusation, and to aggravate what He said, by the act. For since what had been said moved the hearers to fear, what they did about Stephen, stopping their ears, this high priest doth here also.

And yet what kind of blasphemy was this? For indeed before He had said, when they were gathered together, "The Lord said unto my Lord. Sit Thou on my right hand," and interpreted the saying, and they dared say nothing, but held their peace, and from that time forth gainsaid Him no more. Why then did they now call the saying a blasphemy? And wherefore also did Christ thus answer them? To take away all their excuse, because unto the last day He taught that He was Christ, and that He sitteth at the right hand of the Father, and that He will come again to judge the world, which was the language of one manifesting His full accordance with the Father.

Watch for your life's sake. Let not your lamps be quenched, nor your loins unloosed; but be ye ready, for ye know not the hour in which our Lord cometh. But often shall ye come together, seeking the things which are befitting to your souls: for the whole time of your faith will not profit you, if ye be not made perfect in the last time. For in the last days false prophets and corrupters shall be multiplied, and the sheep shall be turned into wolves, and love shall be turned into hate; for when lawlessness increaseth, they shall hate and persecute and betray one another, and then shall appear the world-deceiver as Son of God, and shall do signs and wonders, and the earth shall be delivered into his hands, and he shall do iniquitous things which have never yet come to pass since the beginning. Then shall the creation of men come into the fire of trial, and many shall be made to stumble and shall perish; but they that endure in their faith shall be saved from under the curse itself. And then shall appear the signs of the truth; first, the sign of an out-spreading in heaven; then the sign of the sound of the trumpet; and the third, the resurrection of the dead; yet not of all, but as it is said: The Lord shall come and all His saints with Him. Then shall the world see the Lord coming upon the clouds of heaven.

t: From the Latin Translation of Cassiodorus
q: Now, in the Gospel according to Mark, the Lord being interrogated by the chief of the priests if He was the Christ, the Son of the blessed God, answering, said, "I am; and you shall see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power." But powers mean the holy angels. Further, when He says "at the right hand of God," He means the self-same [beings], by reason of the equality and likeness of the angelic and holy powers, which are called by the name of God. He says, therefore, that He sits at the right hand; that is, that He rests in pre-eminent honour. In the other Gospels, however, He is said not to have replied to the high priest, on his asking if He was the Son of God. But what said He? "You say." Answering sufficiently well. For had He said, It is as you understand, he would have said what was not true, not confessing Himself to be the Son of God; [for] they did not entertain this opinion of Him; but by saying "You say," He spoke truly. For what they had no knowledge of, but expressed in words, that he confessed to be true.

It was not fit that the Lord should answer the High Priest's adjuration as though under compulsion, wherefore He neither denied nor confessed Himself to be the Son of God. For he was not worthy to be the object of Christ's teaching, therefore He does not instruct him, but taking up his own words retorts them upon him. This sitting of the Son of Man seems to me to denote a certain regal security; by the power of God, Who is the only power, is He securely seated to Whom is given by His Father all power in heaven as in earth. And there will come a time when the enemies shall see this establishment. Indeed this has begun to be fulfilled from the earliest time of the dispensation; for the disciples saw Him rising from the dead, and thereby saw Him seated on the right hand of power. Or, In respect of that eternity of duration which is with God, from the beginning of the world to the end of it is but one day; it is therefore no wonder that the Saviour here says, Shortly, signifying that there is but short time before the end come. He prophesies moreover, that they should not only see Him sitting at the right hand of power, but also coming in the clouds of heaven. These clouds are the Prophets and Apostles, whom He commands to rain when it is required, they are the clouds that pass not away, but bearing the image of the heavenly, (1 Cor. 15:49.) are worthy to be the throne of God, as heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ. (Rom. 8:17.)

Yet I say to you: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power, and coming upon the clouds of heaven (26, 64ᵇ).

Since it is not written at the right hand of God, but in all the evangelists at the right hand of the Power (and "of God" is not added), it is worthwhile to discern what it is for the Son of Man to sit at the right hand of the Power. Likewise the three evangelists write similarly: you shall see him sitting; and to the simple, indeed, who can hear nothing lofty in that which he says sitting, it is granted to understand it as if he said "established above the Power." But to those to whom it is possible to search out all things by the Spirit, "even the depths of God," they will understand both what is written: "you who sit upon the cherubim, appear" and: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up" and: "the Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet" and other things of the like. These things that are said of God sitting are likewise also said of Christ. And these ought to be compared with the present saying, so that from a lowly and fabulous estimation we may see what the sitting of Christ signifies after the manner of men. But it seems to me that the sitting of the Son of Man signifies a certain foundation and royal steadfastness. According to the Power, therefore — he who alone is the Power and is properly so named — he is also established at the right hand, he who has received all power from the Father, as "in heaven and on earth"; and this foundation even the adversaries will one day see, after the blessed have with joy seen him.

But according to Mark it does not have from now on, but purely, that is: "you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power"; and according to him there will be nothing contrary to the things we have handed down. But according to Matthew, who says from now on you shall see, and according to Luke, who says "from this time the Son of Man will be" and the rest, it must be inquired whether, from the time the Savior said these things, they were fulfilled also in those who heard what he said: from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power. And we say that it can be seen as fulfilled, since from that time, that is, from the time of the dispensation, the Son of Man sat at the right hand of the Power, and his disciples saw him rising from the dead, and through this they saw him established at the right hand of the Power, according to what we have handed down above. Or thus: see whether you can measure the hour and the day not according to the brevity of hours and days that is among men, but according to the length that is with the eternal Lord, to whom from the foundation of the world until its consummation there is one day — which is demonstrated by the parable, where he speaks of those hired into the vineyard in the morning and at the third hour and the sixth and up to the eleventh. It is therefore no wonder that here the Savior says that from now on until then there is a very short span, in which span he was saying: you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the Power to those who were then hearing him — perhaps then when "the Lord said to my Lord: sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet", among whom were also those to whom he was saying from now on you shall see; for Caiaphas too was an enemy, who was plotting against Christ.

And he was prophesying that these would see him not only sitting at the right hand of the Power, but also would see him coming (as Matthew indeed says) upon the clouds of heaven. But what are the clouds upon which he will come who is established at the right hand of the Power, or with which he will come, or to which the truth of God will reach, according to what is written: "and your truth reaches even to the clouds"? These are the living clouds, the prophets of God and the apostles of Christ, whom he commands to rain when it is fitting, or not to rain upon the vineyard without fruit. But if anyone does not wish to be a cloud of this kind, upon which and with which the Son of Man will come when he appears, let him himself take heed. For he always comes upon those and with those, showing his coming to those worthy of him — God the Word and Wisdom and Truth and Righteousness. And these clouds which we have handed down, as though bearing "the image of the heavenly", are clouds of the heaven that does not pass away, made worthy of the seat of God and the kingdom of God, as "heirs of God and coheirs of Christ", and they reign together with him.

The same fury which drew the High Priest from his seat, impels him now to rend his clothes; for so it was customary with the Jews to do whenever they heard any blasphemy, or any thing against God.

And by this rending his garments, he shows that the Jews have lost the priestly glory, and that their High Priest's throne was vacant. For by rending his garment he rent the veil of the Law which covered him.

Then the chief priest tore his garments, saying: he has blasphemed (26, 65ᵃ).

While the Lord was prophesying these things, that priest, the Lord's enemy — as one who was not near enough to see the Son of Man and the Power at whose right hand he was seated, as one bent down and unable to look upward, not hearing the things he was saying — tore his garments, displaying his own foulness and the nakedness of his soul, and making manifest a mystery: that the old priesthood was to be torn asunder, along with the robe of his priesthood and of the worship which had been according to the letter.

But he judged the greatness of Christ's words to be blasphemy, and he esteemed as glory the Jewish and fabulous history of the letter that kills. And he supposed (as though he understood) that Christ's discourses were sufficient as testimony against him — those very discourses which were witnesses of his divinity (as far as concerns those who are able to understand). And he says to those who were of the same mind: behold, now you have heard his blasphemy; what does it seem to you. Until, answering, they too pronounce against their own soul concerning Jesus, that he is guilty of death. How great, do you think, was the error, to pronounce Life itself, the principal Life of all, guilty of death, and by the testimony of so many rising again not to behold the fountain of life, from which life flowed forth into all the living, seeing that "as the Father has life in himself, so also he has granted to the Son to have life in himself"?

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 84
q:
Having rent therefore his clothes, he saith, "What think ye?" He gives not the sentence from himself, but invites it from them, as in a case of confessed sins, and manifest blasphemy. For, inasmuch as they knew that if the thing came to be inquired into, and carefully decided, it would free Him from all blame, they condemn Him amongst themselves, and anticipate the hearers by saying, "Ye have heard the blasphemy;" all but necessitating and forcing them to deliver the sentence. What then say they? "He is guilty of death;" that having taken Him as condemned, they should thus work upon Pilate thereupon to pass sentence. In which matter those others also being accomplices say, "He is guilty of death;" themselves accusing, themselves judging, themselves passing sentence, themselves being everything then.

But wherefore did they not bring forward the Sabbaths? Because He had often stopped their mouths; and moreover they wanted to take Him, and condemn Him by the things then said. And the high priest anticipated them, and gave the sentence as from them, and drew them all on by rending his vestments, and having led Him away as now condemned unto Pilate, thus did all.

How great their error! to pronounce the principle of all men's life to be guilty of death, and not to acknowledge by the testimony of the resurrection of so many, the Fount of life, from Whom life flows to all that rise again.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85
q:
Wherefore did they these things, when they were to put Him to death? What need of this mockery? That thou mightest learn their intemperate spirit by all things, and that having taken Him like a prey, they thus showed forth their intoxication, and gave full swing to their madness; making this a festival, and assaulting Him with pleasure, and showing forth their murderous disposition.

But admire, I pray thee, the self command of the disciples, with what exactness they relate these things. Hereby is clearly shown their disposition to love the truth, because they relate with all truthfulness the things that seem to be opprobrious, disguising nothing, nor being ashamed thereof, but rather accounting it very great glory, as indeed it was, that the Lord of the universe should endure to suffer such things for us. This shows both His unutterable tenderness, and the inexcusable wickedness of those men, who had the heart to do such things to Him that was so mild and meek, and was charming them with such words, as were enough to change a lion into a lamb. For neither did He fail in any things of gentleness, nor they of insolence and cruelty, in what they did, in what they said.

For what could be equal to this insolence? On that face which the sea, when it saw it, had reverenced, from which the sun, when it beheld it on the cross, turned away his rays, they did spit, and struck it with the palms of their hands, and some upon the head; giving full swing in every way to their own madness. For indeed they inflicted the blows that are most insulting of all, buffeting, smiting with the palms of their hands, and to these blows adding the insult of spitting at Him. And words again teeming with much derision did they speak, saying, "prophesy unto us, thou Christ, who is he that smote thee?" because the multitude called Him a prophet.

But another saith, that they covered His face with His own garment, and did these things, as though they had got in the midst of them some vile and worthless fellow. And not freemen only, but slaves also were intemperate with this intemperance towards Him at that time.

These things let us read continually, these things let us hear aright, these things let us write in our minds, for these are our honors. In these things do I take a pride, not only in the thousands of dead which He raised, but also in the sufferings which He endured. These things Paul puts forward in every way, the cross, the death, the sufferings, the revilings, the insults, the scoffs.

(Quaest. Ev. i. 44.) That, they did spit in his face, signifies those who reject His proffered grace. They likewise buffet Him who prefer their own honour to Him; and they smite Him on the face, who, blinded with unbelief, affirm that He is not yet come, disowning and rejecting His person.
They spit in his face, and buffeted him, to fulfil the prophecy of Esaias, I gave my cheek to the smiters, and turned not away my face from shame and spitting. (Isa. 50:6.)

Then they spat in his face and struck him with their fists. But others slapped his face with the palms of their hands, saying: Prophesy to us, O Christ, who is it that struck you? (26, 67. 68)

Most wickedly, as I judge, did those who had heard Jesus saying: "yet I say to you, that from now on you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming in the clouds of heaven" dare to spit in his face. For they supposed that by this they would confound him as a liar, and that one who sat "at the right hand of power" and was to come "in the clouds" would not endure the reproach of being spat upon; for they were ignorant of the words of the prophet Isaiah, who prophesied these very same things concerning him, and said in the person of the Lord and Savior himself: "what, that I came, and there was no man? I called, and there was none who would obey? Is my hand not able to rescue? Or can I not deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert. And their fish shall be dried up because they have no water, and shall die of thirst. And I will clothe the heaven with darkness, and make its covering like sackcloth. The Lord gives me the tongue of instruction, that I may know how it behooves me to speak the word; he set me in the morning, he applied to me an ear to hear, and the instruction of the Lord shall open my ears; but I am not unbelieving, nor do I contradict. I offered my back to the scourges, and my cheeks to the palms of hands, but I did not turn away my face from the confusion of spittings, and the Lord God became my helper". For all who are of the Church confess him to be Christ who says: "the Lord, the Lord gave me the tongue of instruction" and the rest which I have expounded.

But I have fittingly expounded also those things which above were joined to these, wishing to show that this was prophesied concerning that glorious one, that he should be spat upon and buffeted. For to what other does it fit to say: "I came", except to Christ who came into the world? Or whom did it befit to say: "I called, and there was none who would obey", except him who came to call the people of the Jews and was not heard, and therefore did not rescue the people nor deliver it, but forsook it? And it is Christ who says: "behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea a desert, and I will set the rivers a desert", who is to bring about the consummation of the world. For it is he who will clothe the heaven with "darkness" and clothe it "as with sackcloth", and, receiving from the Father the "tongue of instruction", knew how "it behooved him to speak the word" which God had entrusted to him; and "he applied to him an ear", that he might hear more than all who hear, and the "instruction" of the Father opened his ear, because he was not unbelieving to the Father who sent him nor contradicting, and by the very deed he taught those desiring to learn meekness and praiseworthy humility. And there was a work in this, that he taught these things by deeds, offering his "back to the scourges and his cheeks to the palms of hands" and not turning away his face "from the confusion of spittings", so that us (as I judge), who had all been worthy to suffer these disgraces, he himself might rescue by suffering them for us. For he did "not die for us", that we might not die, but that we might not die for ourselves; and he was struck with blows for us and was spat upon, so that we, who had been worthy of all these things on account of our sins, might not suffer them, but that, suffering them for righteousness, we might receive them gladly. And Paul indeed says of the Savior, that "he humbled himself, being made obedient unto death, even the death of the cross". For it is not unseemly for one who wishes to number in how many things Christ humbled himself, to count out (beyond those things which Paul expounded, saying: "he humbled himself, being made obedient unto death"): unto the "palms of hands", unto the "confusion of spittings" and of "scourges" and of death, on account of all which "God exalted him". For it was not on account of death alone which he bore for us that he exalted him, but also on account of the palms and the spittings and the rest.

But that the injury of spittings is taken as the extreme injury, is manifest also in the law, in which it is written that the wife of a deceased man, if the brother of her husband will not take her, going to him who refused to take her to himself as wife, in the presence of the elders shall unshoe "one of his sandals from his feet and shall spit in his face and shall say: so shall it be done to the man who has not built up the house of his brother". Therefore Christ did not turn away his face "from the confusion of spittings", that his countenance might be more glorified than the countenance of Moses was glorified, with so great and such glory that (by comparison with this glorification) the glorification of that countenance is done away, just as in the sight of the sun the light of a lamp is done away, and just as the knowledge which is in part is done away "when that which is perfect has come". But they also struck with their fists the holy head of the Church, on account of which they themselves are buffeted by Satan, not that they may not be exalted nor that their strength may be made perfect, but that, handed over to the enemy and avenger, they may receive back the sin which they committed in buffeting Jesus. And not content only to spit in his face and to strike him with their fists, they still further struck him with the palms of their hands and, mocking him, said: prophesy to us, who struck you. On account of which they received an eternal blow, and were deprived of all prophecy, struck and chastised, and even so not willing to receive instruction, according to what Jeremiah had prophesied of this very thing concerning them: "you scourged them and they did not grieve, and they refused to receive instruction". And now those who do injury to some one person of the Church and do these things to him, spit in the face of Christ and, striking Christ with their fists, chastise him also with the palms of their hands.
But it would have been foolish to have answered them that smote Him, and to have declared the smiter, seeing that in their madness they seem to have struck Him openly.

t: Homily on the Gospel of Matthew 85
q:
Oh strange and wonderful acts! When indeed he saw his master seized only, he was so fervent as both to draw his sword, and to cut off the man's ear; but when it was natural for him to be more indignant, and to be inflamed and to burn, hearing such revilings, then he becomes a denier. For who would not have been inflamed to madness by the things that were then doing? yet the disciple, overcome by fears, so far from showing indignation, even denies, and endures not the threat of a miserable and mean girl, and not once only, but a second and third time doth he deny Him; and in a short period, and not so much as before judges, for it was without for "when he had gone out into the porch," they asked him, and he did not even readily come to a sense of his fall. And this Luke saith, namely, that Christ looked on him showing that he not only denied Him, but was not even brought to remembrance from within, and this though the cock had crowed; but he needed a further remembrance from his master, and His look was to him instead of a voice; so exceedingly was he full of fear.

But Mark saith, that when he had once denied, then first the cock crew, but when thrice, then for the second time; for he declares more particularly the weakness of the disciple, and that he was utterly dead with fear; having learnt these things of his masters himself, for he was a follower of Peter. In which respect one would most marvel at him, that so far from hiding his teacher's faults, he declared it more distinctly than the rest, on this very account, that he was his disciple.

How then is what is said true, when Matthew affirms that Christ said, "Verily I say unto thee, that before the cock crow thou shalt deny me thrice;" and Mark declares after the third denial, that "The cock crew the second time?" Nay, most certainly is it both true and in harmony. For because at each crowing the cock is wont to crow both a third and a fourth time, Mark, to show that not even the sound checked him, and brought him to recollection saith this. So that both things are true. For before the cock had finished the one crowing, he had denied a third time. And not even when reminded of his sin by Christ did he dare to weep openly, lest he should be betrayed by his tears, but "he went out, and wept bitterly."

(de Cons. Ev. iii. 6.) Among the other insults offered to our Lord was the threefold denial of Peter, which the several Evangelists relate in different order. Luke puts Peter's trial first, and the ill usage of the Lord after that; Matthew and Mark reverse the order.

(ubi sup.) We understand that having gone out after his first denial, the cock crowed the first time as Mark relates.

(ubi sup.) The second denial was not outside the door, but after he had returned to the fire; for the second maid did not see him after he had gone out, but as he was going out; his getting up to go out drew her attention, and she said to them that were there, that is, to those that were standing round the fire in the hall, Tins fellow also was with Jesus of Nazareth. He who had gone out, haying heard this returned, that he might by denial vindicate himself. Or, as is more likely, he did not hear what was said of him as he went out, but it was after he came back that the maid, and the other man whom Luke mentions, said to him, And thou also art one of them.

(ubi sup.) Let us now come to the third denial; And after a while came they that stood by, and said to Peter, Surely thou also art one of them, (Luke's words are, About the space of one hour after,) for thy speech bewrayeth thee. (Luke 22:59.)

(Quæst. Ev. i. 45.) Also Peter thrice denied, because heretical error concerning Christ is limited to three kinds; they are in error respecting His divinity, His humanity, or both.
Peter sat without, that he might see the event, and not excite suspicion by any approach to Jesus.

(Serm. 60, 4.) For this reason it should seem he was permitted to waver, that the remedy of penitence might be exhibited in the head of the Church, and that none should dare to trust in his own strength, when even the blessed Peter could not escape the danger of frailty.

Observe how baneful are communications with evil men; they even drove Peter to deny the Lord whom he had before confessed to be the Son of God.

Spiritually; By Peter's denial before the cock-crow, are denoted those who before Christ's resurrection did not believe Him to be God, being perplexed by His death. In his denial after the first cock-crow, are denoted those who are in error concerning both Christ's natures, His human and divine. By the first handmaid is signified desire; by the second, carnal delight; by them that stood by, the dæmons; for by them men are led to a denial of Christ.

Or, By the first handmaid is understood the Synagogue of the Jews, which oft compelled the faithful to deny; by the second, the congregations of the Gentiles, who even persecuted the Christians; they that stood in the hall signify the ministers of divers heresies, who also compel men to deny the truth of Christ.

But Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard; and one of the maidservants came to him, saying: You too were with Jesus the Galilean. But he denied it before them all, saying: I do not know what you are saying. And as he was going out to the gate, another maidservant saw him and said to him there: This man too was with Jesus the Nazarene. And again he denied it with an oath, saying, I do not know the man. And after a little while those who were standing there came and said to Peter: Truly you are one of them, for even your speech makes you plain. Then he began to curse and to swear, saying, I do not know the man. And immediately a cock crowed. And Peter remembered the word of Jesus who had said to him: Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times; and going out he wept most bitterly.

Considering Peter's denial more fully, we say that "no one can call Jesus Lord except in the Holy Spirit" (as Paul teaches us), and "the Holy Spirit was not yet then" in men "because Jesus had not yet been glorified" (as John says), and therefore it was not possible that even such a Peter should then confess Jesus. Nor yet was he to be blamed for not confessing Jesus, since to those who confess it is said: "It is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you".

But we, since that Spirit of our Father is able to speak in us, and since it is in our power to give "place" in us to the Holy Spirit and not to "the devil", if we deny him, we shall have no excuse.

Perhaps, moreover, whoever is in the courtyard of Caiaphas "the chief priest" cannot confess the Lord Jesus unless he has gone out of his courtyard and been made to be outside of every doctrine that is contrary to Jesus and that hands down Jewish traditions—and this not according to the will of the Scriptures, but according to "the commandments and teachings of men". For consider that Peter, sitting outside, separated from Jesus and set in the courtyard of the chief priest, denied Jesus before them all; and again a second time, likewise, being not yet made to be outside beyond the gate, but wishing to go out and not yet having gone out, denied him at the gate; but also a third time, when those who were standing said: Truly you are one of them, and when he began to curse himself and to swear, saying, I do not know the man, he was still not outside. And all these denials were made by him in the night and in darkness, before day comes and the sign of day, that is, the cock's crow which rouses from sleep those who are willing. And, to speak by way of example, if Peter had denied him after the cock's crow—so that it might be said: "the night has advanced, and the day has drawn near, let us walk becomingly as in the day"—Peter would have been worthy of no excuse.

But perhaps also all men, when they deny Jesus in such a way that the sin of their denial may receive healing, are seen to deny him before the cock's crow, when the sun of righteousness has not yet risen upon them nor its rising drawn near to them. But if, after the rising of such a sun upon the soul, "we sin willingly after we have received the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains for us a sacrifice for sin, but a fearful judgment and a zeal of fire, which is to consume the enemies".

And indeed in the case of Peter, then denying, it was not fitting to say: "how do you not think that they deserve worse punishments who have trodden underfoot the Son of God and have esteemed the blood of the covenant common, by which they were sanctified, and have done injury to the Spirit of grace?"; for Peter had not yet been sanctified by the blood of Christ (which was the blood of the new covenant), nor did he do injury to the Spirit of grace which from the beginning he had not even received, since "Jesus had not yet been glorified", "nor was" the "Holy Spirit" in men.

But if in us this impious sin of denial has been committed, it is fitting to say all these things, since we have both been sanctified by the blood of the covenant and have received the "Spirit of grace". Therefore to esteem the most precious "blood of the covenant" as "common" and to do injury to the Spirit of grace is worse than all sins, so that we can receive remission "neither in this age nor in the age to come", if we deny the Son of God. Since therefore for us "the night has advanced, and the day has drawn near" and the sign of day, the cock's crow, has sounded to us, therefore let us stand "even unto blood, contending against sin", and for the sake of the charity that never falls away let us endure all things, that with those perfected in it we may obtain the inheritance. And mark this, that before the cock's crow, and before the Holy Spirit, and in the time of deep night, even if someone should deny frequently, he can live; which is plain from the fact that Peter denied three times. But if after the cock's crow someone, even once, being set in whatever peril, should deny, "it is impossible for him to be renewed unto repentance, so as to crucify again to himself the Son of God".
