But whoever has been caught in such a sin of denial, let him look upon that which is written: "woe to those who draw their sins to themselves as with a long rope, and their iniquities as with the strap of a yoke of a calf", and let him not say: "our sins are upon us, and how shall we live? As I live, says the Lord, since I do not will the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance". But God himself knows—of whom it is written: "and he, being wise, will bring evils upon them"—what kind of evils he will bring upon those who deny and do not repent, and what kind upon those who deny and do repent, and what kind of good things upon those who have never denied him either in word "before men" or in works. And let us become far removed from the first maidservant and from the other, and from all who stand in his courtyard or at his gate, that we may not be near to those who cause the one who is beside them to deny him. But we shall know who the maidservant of the chief priest is, if we understand who the maidservant of God is, of whom it is written: "I am your servant and the son of your maidservant".

And you will be able to know what the courtyards of the chief priest are, if you understand what the courtyards of the house of God are, of which it is written: "behold now, bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord", "you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courtyards of the house of our God". But if we must also say something about the other maidservant, so that we may withdraw from her as well, let us understand what is written: "as the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so are our eyes toward the Lord our God, until he have mercy upon us". I think the first maidservant of the chief priest, who causes the disciples of Christ to deny him, is to be understood as the synagogue of the Jews "according to the flesh", who have frequently compelled the faithful to deny; and the second maidservant as the assembly of the Gentiles, who, themselves also persecuting Christians, compelled them to deny; and the third, those standing in the courtyards, are the ministers of the various heresies, who themselves also compel men to deny the truth of Christ. But in the night Peter not only denies three times, but even curses himself and swears that I do not know the man. And indeed then he still knew Christ "according to the flesh", nor could he yet say: "even if we have known Christ at some time according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him thus"; for as long as the sign of day did not yet exist, Peter in denying was not mindful of the words of Jesus, but after the angel of day cried out to him, then he remembered the word of Jesus who said to him: before the cock crows, you will deny me three times. And when he remembered the word of Christ, he was no longer in the courtyard of the chief priest nor beside his gate, but outside; otherwise he would by no means have wept, for thus it is written: going out he wept most bitterly. Therefore, as according to Luke the "sinful woman" beside the feet of the Lord "wept" in repentance, so here Peter, having gone out of the courtyard of the chief priest to his gate, weeps from the bitterness of sin, making his weeping bitter in repentance.
(in Luc. 22, 57.) I had rather that Peter deny, than that the Lord be made out false.

And again he denied with an oath, I do not know the man. I know that some out of a feeling of piety towards the Apostle Peter have interpreted this place to signify that Peter denied the Man and not the God, as though he meant, 'I do not know the Man, because I know the God.' But the intelligent reader will see that this is trifling, for if he denied not, the Lord spoke falsely when He said, Thou shalt deny me thrice.
Not that Peter was of a different speech or nation, but a Hebrew as his accusers were; but every province and every district has its peculiarities, and he could not disguise his native pronunciation.

In another Gospel we read, that after Peter's denial and the cock-crow, the Saviour looked upon Peter, (Luke 22:61.) and by His look called forth those bitter tears; for it might not be that he on whom the Light of the world had looked should continue in the darkness of denial, wherefore, he went out, and wept bitterly. For he could not do penitence sitting in Caiaphas' hall, but went forth from the assembly of the wicked, that he might wash away in bitter tears the pollution of his timid denial.

(Serm. 60. 4.) Blessed tears, O holy Apostle, which had the virtue of holy Baptism in washing off the sin of thy denial. The right hand of the Lord Jesus Christ was with thee to hold thee up before thou wast quite thrown down, and in the midst of thy perilous fall, thou receivedst strength to stand. The Rock quickly returned to its stability, recovering so great fortitude, that he who in Christ's passion had quailed, should endure his own subsequent suffering with fearlessness and constancy.
